claims.text: Marion was a coastal city-kingdom on the northwest tip of Cyprus, with a sanctuary of a fertility goddess in continuous use from around the tenth to the early fifth century BC.
Marion is sometimes identified with "Nuria," one of ten kingdoms named on a prism of the Assyrian king Esarhaddon recording tribute paid around 673 BC.
Ptolemy I destroyed Marion in 312 BC for siding with his rival Antigonus, and Ptolemy II refounded a new city nearby as Arsinoe, named for his sister-wife.

summary: A copper-trade city-kingdom on Cyprus's northwest tip, destroyed for backing the losing side in the wars after Alexander's death and refounded under a new name.
significance: Its identification as one of the ten kingdoms named in Esarhaddon's tribute list is a useful example of how much of Cyprus's early political geography rests on scholarly reconstruction of garbled foreign transliterations, not settled fact.
body:
Marion controlled the northwest corner of Cyprus and its access to copper-bearing districts, prospering on a trade that shows up archaeologically in over 850 excavated tombs and centuries of sanctuary activity. A rural sanctuary at nearby Peristeries, dedicated to a female fertility goddess, was in continuous use from roughly the tenth to the early fifth century BC, and a probable palace building of the sixth century BC has also been identified.

A clay prism of the Assyrian king Esarhaddon lists ten Cypriot kings who paid him tribute around 673 BC, giving each a garbled Akkadian rendering of a Cypriot royal name and city. Modern scholars have matched most of these names to known kingdoms with reasonable confidence, but one entry, "Nuria," is only tentatively equated with Marion — a guess based on process of elimination rather than direct evidence, and this entity's status among the ten kingdoms should be read as contested rather than settled.

In 312 BC, during the wars between Alexander's former generals, Marion's king backed Antigonus against Ptolemy I, who took the city and had it destroyed. Ptolemy II later founded a new city nearby, naming it Arsinoe after his sister and wife — one of several Cypriot cities renamed for Ptolemaic royal women in this period.

name: Lapithos

claims.text: Lapithos was a north-coast city-kingdom of Cyprus, with cemeteries documenting continuous occupation from around 3000 BC.

Lapithos does not appear among the ten Cypriot kingdoms named in Esarhaddon's tribute-list prism of around 673 BC; it is instead listed as one of nine Cypriot kingdoms in a later, separate tradition recorded by the Greek historian Diodorus Siculus.
Ptolemy I absorbed Lapithos's kingdom in 312 BC, in the same campaign that destroyed Marion.

summary: A north-coast kingdom whose deep cemetery record stretches back to the Chalcolithic, though its place among Cyprus's "ten kingdoms" is a separate, later tradition rather than the Assyrian tribute list most of the others share.
significance: Its necropoleis anchor the pottery sequence archaeologists use to date the transition from Bronze to Iron Age Cyprus.
body:
Lapithos lies on Cyprus's north coast, in the shadow of the Kyrenia mountain range. The Vrysi tou Barba and Kastros cemeteries, excavated by the Swedish Cyprus Expedition, yielded more than 75 Bronze Age chamber tombs whose Bichrome Red pottery sequence remains a key reference point for dating the wider transition from the Bronze Age to the Iron Age on Cyprus.

Ancient lists of Cyprus's city-kingdoms are not fully consistent with one another. The best-known list, ten kings named on a prism of the Assyrian king Esarhaddon recording tribute paid around 673 BC, does not include Lapithos. It appears instead in a separate, later tradition recorded by the Greek historian Diodorus Siculus, describing nine Cypriot kingdoms in the context of events centuries after Esarhaddon's prism was inscribed. The two traditions are sometimes run together in popular accounts of "the ten kingdoms of Cyprus," but they describe different moments and, in places, different sets of cities.

Like several other independent kingdoms, Lapithos lost its autonomy in 312 BC when Ptolemy I moved against Cypriot rulers who had backed his rival Antigonus in the wars following Alexander's death.

name: Enkomi

claims.text: Enkomi was a major fortified Late Bronze Age city and copper-trade hub, one of the largest settlements on Cyprus in this period.
Enkomi is a leading candidate for the site of Alashiya, a major copper-exporting polity named in Late Bronze Age Egyptian and Near Eastern diplomatic correspondence.
Cypro-Minoan script tablets found at Enkomi, including the longest known example of the script, are key evidence for literacy on Late Bronze Age Cyprus.
Enkomi was abandoned around 1050 BC and its population is thought to have shifted to nearby Salamis, though the exact mechanism -- earthquake, harbour siltation, or another cause -- is debated.

milestones.text: The British Museum excavates tombs at the site.
Porphyrios Dikaios excavates the Late Bronze Age town.

summary: A major Late Bronze Age copper-trading city a few kilometres from where Salamis later rose, and a strong candidate for the elusive kingdom of Alashiya.
significance: Its bronze cult statuettes, Cypro-Minoan tablets and dense ashlar architecture are central evidence for how thoroughly Late Bronze Age Cyprus was integrated into the wider eastern Mediterranean copper trade.
body:
Enkomi stood a few kilometres inland from Cyprus's east coast, near modern Famagusta, at the head of a lagoon that then gave it direct harbour access. Excavations, principally French and British missions through the twentieth century, uncovered dense ashlar-built architecture, a sanctuary yielding the bronze "Ingot God" and "Horned God" statuettes, and roughly two thousand tombs.

Egyptian and other Near Eastern diplomatic correspondence of the fourteenth and thirteenth centuries BC repeatedly mentions a copper-rich land called Alashiya. Enkomi is one of the strongest candidates for its capital, though the identification rests on circumstantial evidence -- the city's scale, its metalworking industry and its trade connections -- rather than a text found on Cyprus itself naming the place.

Tablets in the undeciphered Cypro-Minoan script, including the longest example yet found, show that Enkomi's administration used writing, though what the script actually records remains largely unknown. The city was abandoned around 1050 BC, in the same period of disruption across the eastern Mediterranean associated with the Bronze Age collapse; its population is generally thought to have relocated to nearby Salamis, though whether an earthquake, the silting of its harbour, or some other cause forced the move is not settled.

name: Hala Sultan Tekke

claims.text: Hala Sultan Tekke was one of the largest Late Bronze Age cities in the Mediterranean, covering an estimated 25 to 50 hectares beside the Larnaca Salt Lake.
Imported goods found there span from Sardinia and Scandinavia to Mesopotamia and Egypt, indicating a wide trading network built substantially on copper and purple-dye textiles.
The site was destroyed or abandoned around the twelfth century BC, in the period of wider disruption across the eastern Mediterranean known as the Late Bronze Age collapse.

milestones.text: The British Museum excavates tombs at the site.
Paul Åström begins a long Swedish excavation of the harbour town.

summary: One of the largest cities of the Late Bronze Age Mediterranean, its harbour trade reaching from Scandinavia to Mesopotamia, now largely invisible above ground beside a salt lake near Larnaca.
significance: Long-running Swedish excavations and geophysical survey have mapped a city on a scale that reframes how urbanised Late Bronze Age Cyprus actually was.
body:
Hala Sultan Tekke -- named for a later Ottoman-era mosque nearby, unrelated to the Bronze Age remains beneath the modern name -- lay on what was then a natural harbour beside the Larnaca Salt Lake, since silted and cut off from the sea. At an estimated 25 to 50 hectares it ranks among the largest urban settlements known anywhere in the Late Bronze Age Mediterranean.

Decades of excavation by the University of Gothenburg, combined with georadar and magnetometer survey of unexcavated areas, have identified multiple distinct city quarters, a cemetery, and probable fortification walls. The material recovered is strikingly international: imports and exports connect the city to Sardinia and Scandinavia in the west and Mesopotamia and Egypt in the east, built on a local economy of copper working and purple-dye textile production.

Like many Late Bronze Age centres across the eastern Mediterranean, Hala Sultan Tekke was destroyed or abandoned during the twelfth century BC, the period of widespread disruption conventionally associated with the "Sea Peoples" and the broader Bronze Age collapse. Unlike Enkomi, its population's fate afterward is not clearly tied to any specific successor settlement.

name: Vouni Palace

claims.text: The palace at Vouni was built on a hilltop above Soloi around 500 BC, apparently by a pro-Persian ruler positioned to watch over the rebellious kingdom below.
Excavation of the palace produced the "Vouni Treasure," including gold bracelets counted among the finest surviving examples of Achaemenid-period goldwork.
The palace's pottery assemblage mixes Persian and Greek styles, reflecting Cyprus's position between the two cultural spheres under Achaemenid rule.

milestones.text: The Swedish Cyprus Expedition excavates the palace.

summary: A hilltop palace built, it seems, to keep watch on a rebellious neighbour -- and a showcase for the finest Achaemenid-period goldwork found on Cyprus.
significance: Its mixed Persian and Greek material culture is some of the clearest physical evidence for how Cypriot elites navigated Achaemenid overlordship.
body:
Vouni occupies a defensible hill on Cyprus's northwest coast, close enough to Soloi to have overlooked it directly. The palace's construction is generally connected to the aftermath of the Ionian Revolt-era Cypriot uprising against Persian rule around 497 BC, in which Soloi held out longer than any other Cypriot city under siege -- the likeliest explanation for why a pro-Persian ruler, possibly installed at nearby Marion, would build a fortified residence positioned to watch it.

Excavated by the Swedish Cyprus Expedition, the palace went through several building phases across the fifth and fourth centuries BC before its abandonment or destruction around 380 BC. Its most celebrated find, the so-called Vouni Treasure, includes gold bracelets ranked among the finest examples of Achaemenid-period goldwork found anywhere, alongside silver vessels. The wider pottery assemblage mixes Persian and Greek forms and styles, physical evidence of a Cypriot elite operating between two cultural and political worlds rather than belonging cleanly to either.

name: Choirokoitia

claims.text: Choirokoitia was a large aceramic Neolithic village of circular stone-built dwellings (tholoi), among the best-preserved prehistoric settlements in the eastern Mediterranean.
The dead were commonly buried beneath the floors of houses, often with stone slabs or querns placed on the body.
Only part of the site has been excavated, leaving an unusually large intact archaeological reserve for future study.
The precise date at which the settlement was finally abandoned, and whether it was continuously occupied throughout its history or reoccupied after a gap, remains debated.

milestones.text: Porphyrios Dikaios begins excavating the Neolithic village.
Inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

summary: A Neolithic village of circular stone houses, among the best-preserved prehistoric settlements anywhere in the eastern Mediterranean -- and, at up to nine thousand years old, far older than anything else this site maps.
significance: Its scale and preservation make it one of the most important sources anywhere for how people in the eastern Mediterranean lived before farming societies had cities, writing or metal tools.
body:
Choirokoitia occupies a defensible hillside above the Maroni river in southern Cyprus. Excavations beginning with Porphyrios Dikaios in the 1930s, and continued by French missions from the 1970s onward, exposed a dense cluster of circular, stone-founded dwellings known as tholoi, some with upper storeys of mudbrick, connected by narrow paved streets and enclosed by defensive walls.

The dead were typically buried beneath the floors of the houses they had lived in, sometimes with a stone slab or grinding quern placed over the body -- one of several practices that, together with the settlement's isolation on an island already some 60 kilometres from the nearest mainland coast at this date, has made Choirokoitia a key case study for how early farming communities organised themselves.

Only a portion of the roughly 3-hectare site has been excavated. The remainder survives as an intact archaeological reserve, and the settlement's precise chronology -- whether occupation was continuous across its multi-millennium history or interrupted and resumed -- remains a subject of ongoing study. Choirokoitia was inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1998.

Its dates fall entirely before 3200 BC, the earliest year this site's timeline and maps track, so Choirokoitia does not appear as a marker on them -- it predates the Bronze Age world the rest of this dataset covers by millennia.

name: Aegina

claims.text: Aegina struck some of the earliest Greek coins, the silver "turtle" staters, in the sixth century BC.
The Temple of Aphaia was built about 500 BC; its pediment sculptures are now in Munich.
Herodotus reports a long war between Aegina and Athens in the decades before Marathon.
The Aeginetans fought at Salamis and were awarded the prize of valour among the Greeks.
In 431 BC the Athenians expelled the Aeginetan population and resettled the island with their own citizens.
Pindar wrote more odes for Aeginetan victors than for any other city.

summary: Island power in the Saronic Gulf, an early coin-issuer and sea trader, and Athens's bitter neighbour.
significance: Aegina shows that Athens did not have a naval monopoly before 480 BC, and that maritime rivalry drove the building of the Athenian fleet.
body:
Aegina lies in the Saronic Gulf, within sight of Athens. Its soil is poor, and its people turned to the sea: by the sixth century it was among the most prosperous trading states in Greece, with contacts across the Aegean and in Egypt. Its silver coins, stamped with a sea turtle, were among the first in mainland Greece, and the Aeginetan weight standard was widely used, notably in the Peloponnese.

Aegina was Athens's oldest rival. Herodotus tells a tangled story of a feud that began with a dispute over statues of two goddesses and turned into raids and reprisals, and he gives it as part of the background to Athenian naval building. When Persia demanded submission in 491, Aegina complied; Athens complained to Sparta, and King Cleomenes came to arrest the medisers. Yet when Xerxes arrived in 480 the Aeginetans fought bravely at Salamis and were named the best-performing state.

The Temple of Aphaia, built around 500 BC on a ridge above the sea, is one of the best-preserved Doric temples in Greece, and its pedimental sculptures, taken to Munich in 1811, show the shift from the archaic to the early classical style in the two gables. Pindar composed odes for Aeginetan victors in athletic contests, which give a sense of the island's cultural self-image, one based on descent from the heroes Aiakos and Achilles.

Athens brought Aegina into its empire in 457 and evicted its population in 431, settling the island with Athenians. Sparta settled the exiles at Thyrea. Aegina never recovered its earlier standing.

name: Eretria

claims.text: Eretria was one of the leading Greek cities in the eighth century BC and took part in early overseas settlement.
Thucydides mentions a war between Chalcis and Eretria in which much of the Greek world took sides; its date and nature are unclear.
Eretria sent five ships to support the Ionian Revolt in 498 BC.
The Persians took and burned Eretria in 490 BC, and deported many of its people.
Swiss archaeologists have excavated at Eretria since the 1960s, revealing a sanctuary of Apollo Daphnephoros.

summary: Euboean city that helped to found colonies in the eighth century BC and paid for supporting the Ionians when Persia burned it in 490 BC.
significance: Eretria illustrates the early Greek expansion, and its destruction was the immediate prelude to Marathon.
body:
Eretria stood on the western coast of Euboea, across from Attica, a few kilometres from the Bronze Age and Dark Age site at Lefkandi. Lefkandi was abandoned around 700 BC, just as Eretria grew, and many scholars argue that its people moved there; the evidence is circumstantial. Eretria and its neighbour Chalcis were among the most active Greek cities of the early eighth century, sending settlers and traders east and west, and many of the first Greek finds in Italy and the Levant have Euboean origins.

The two cities are said to have fought the Lelantine War for control of the fertile plain between them. Thucydides calls it a war in which the rest of Greece took sides, but he gives no details, and modern historians disagree on whether it was one long conflict, several, or something that never happened as later writers imagined it.

Eretria's sympathy with the Ionians brought disaster. In 498 it sent ships to help the revolt, which ended in the burning of Sardis. Darius resolved to punish Athens and Eretria, and in 490 the Persian force landed on Euboea, besieged Eretria for six days, and took it by treachery. The temples were burned, the citizens deported to Ardericca in Persia, and the fleet then crossed to Marathon. Herodotus adds that the exiles were still speaking Greek in his own day.

Excavation by the Swiss School at Athens has recovered a large part of the city, including a well-preserved late Archaic temple of Apollo with a pediment showing Theseus carrying off the Amazon Antiope. The city was rebuilt after 490 and survived until Roman times.

name: Croton

claims.text: Croton was founded by Achaean settlers around 710 BC, traditionally led by Myscellus of Rhypes on the advice of Delphi.
Pythagoras settled at Croton around 530 BC and founded a community there.
Croton destroyed neighbouring Sybaris in 510 BC.
The wrestler Milo of Croton won six Olympic victories and Crotonians dominated the athletic events in the late sixth century.
The physician Democedes of Croton served at the court of Darius of Persia.
A single column of the Temple of Hera Lacinia still stands at Capo Colonna.

summary: Achaean colony in southern Italy, famed for its athletes and doctors, and home to Pythagoras's community.
significance: Croton shows the intellectual and athletic weight of the western Greeks, and it is the setting for the earliest well-attested Pythagorean society.
body:
Croton was founded on the Ionian coast of Calabria, traditionally about 710 BC, by settlers from Achaea in the northern Peloponnese. Strabo preserves the foundation story: Myscellus was told by Delphi to go where he found rain in fine weather, and was surprised when a woman he loved wept beside him. Its neighbour Sybaris, also Achaean and larger, dominated the coast at first.

By the late sixth century Croton was famous for two things. One was athletics: Crotonians took so many prizes at Olympia that it was said to be the healthiest place in Greece, and Milo, a six-times champion, became a byword for strength. The other was medicine. Democedes of Croton, whom Herodotus describes as the best doctor of his time, cured Darius of a sprain when Egyptian physicians had failed, and stayed at the Persian court as a virtual prisoner until he escaped home.

Pythagoras arrived about 530 BC and drew followers among the elite. The community that grew from his teaching combined philosophy, mathematics and ascetic rules, and it became politically influential. After Croton defeated and razed Sybaris in 510, quarrels over the division of the spoil and the influence of the Pythagoreans led to a revolt against them. Later sources place attacks on Pythagorean meeting houses at various dates and give conflicting stories of what happened to the founder.

In the third century Croton suffered from Bruttian, Syracusan and Roman pressure, and by the time of Hannibal it was much diminished. At Capo Colonna, the temple of Hera Lacinia, once its chief sanctuary, has one standing column.

name: The Academy

claims.text: Plato founded a school in a public gymnasium and grove outside Athens around 387 BC.
The site was named for the hero Akademos and was sacred ground.
After Plato, the school was led by Speusippus and Xenocrates, and later took a sceptical turn under Arcesilaus.
Excavations in the modern park of Akadimia Platonos have uncovered remains of the gymnasium's buildings.
Sulla's army cut down the trees of the Academy for siege equipment in 86 BC.
A Neoplatonist school was active at Athens in the fifth and sixth centuries AD; the closure ordered by Justinian in AD 529 is itself debated.

milestones.text: Panagiotis Aristophron excavates the area at his own expense, finding the road from the Dipylon gate and a large building.

summary: Plato's school outside Athens, in a sacred grove, which shaped Western thought for nine centuries.
significance: The Academy is the model for the university: an organised community for teaching and research that outlived its founder by centuries.
body:
Around 387 BC Plato bought or rented ground near a public gymnasium about a kilometre and a half north-west of Athens, in a grove dedicated to the hero Akademos. There he taught for some forty years. Unlike the Sophists, he did not charge for lessons, and the school was organised as a community of scholars united by shared inquiry into mathematics, dialectic and politics. Aristotle joined at seventeen and stayed for twenty years.

After Plato's death in 347 his nephew Speusippus took over, followed by Xenocrates. The "Old Academy" concentrated on metaphysics and mathematics. In the third century, under Arcesilaus, the school turned sceptical, defending the view that nothing can be known with certainty. This "New Academy" argued against the Stoics until the first century BC, when Antiochus of Ascalon returned to a more dogmatic Platonism.

The grounds were damaged in 86 BC, when Sulla besieged Athens and cut down the groves for siege engines. Teaching went on, however, in the city. In the fifth century AD a Neoplatonist school led by Plutarch of Athens and later Proclus revived the name and claimed descent from Plato. Justinian's edict of AD 529 forbade pagans to teach, and is traditionally seen as the end of the Academy, though historians debate how far it affected the school and whether teaching continued.

The site has been excavated since the 1930s in what is now a public park. The remains are of a gymnasium, a palaestra and associated buildings, which show that the Academy was a physical place used for exercise and teaching as well as philosophy. No building specifically identified as Plato's school has been found.

name: The Lyceum

claims.text: Aristotle founded his school at the Lyceum, a gymnasium sacred to Apollo Lykeios, in 335 BC.
The school was also called the Peripatos because of its covered walk, the peripatos, where the members taught and talked.
Theophrastus led the school after Aristotle, and Strato of Lampsacus after him.
The school carried out systematic research in biology, history, politics and literature, supported by a collection of texts.
Excavations in central Athens in 1996 uncovered part of the Lyceum's palaestra, which is now an archaeological park.
Sulla's siege in 86 BC damaged the Lyceum; the school's decline in later Hellenistic times is widely accepted, though the details are uncertain.

milestones.text: Remains of the gymnasium are found during construction of a museum in central Athens.
The site opens to the public as an archaeological park.

summary: Aristotle's school in a gymnasium sacred to Apollo, from which the Peripatetics carried out organised research.
significance: The Lyceum turned Aristotle's programme of collecting and classifying knowledge into a lasting institution.
body:
The Lyceum lay on the eastern side of Athens, outside the city walls, near a shrine of Apollo Lykeios. It was a public gymnasium, and Aristotle, who was not an Athenian citizen and could not own property, used it when he returned to Athens in 335 BC after tutoring Alexander. He taught in the covered walk, the peripatos, which gave his followers the name Peripatetics.

The school was more research institute than teaching circle. Aristotle and his associates gathered information on a large scale: descriptions of animals and plants, constitutions of Greek cities, records of dramatic contests, and histories of earlier philosophers. Diogenes Laertius records that the members ate together and held a monthly banquet, with rules for the conduct of the school. When Aristotle left Athens in 322 BC, Theophrastus took over and inherited the books.

The Lyceum flourished under Theophrastus and then declined. Strato of Lampsacus, who led it after 288, was interested in physics and natural science, but later heads were less distinguished. By the first century BC Athens was more famous for the Stoics and Epicureans, and a story about the loss and recovery of Aristotle's library in a cellar in Asia Minor, told by Strabo and Plutarch, explains why his lecture-notes were published only in the first century BC by Andronicus of Rhodes.

The gymnasium's remains were discovered in 1996 during the construction of a museum in central Athens. The excavated area includes a palaestra, a courtyard for wrestling, with rooms for changing and bathing. It has been open to the public as an archaeological park since 2014.

name: The Painted Stoa

claims.text: The Painted Stoa was a colonnade on the north side of the Athenian Agora, built about 460 BC.
It displayed paintings of the Battle of Marathon, the Trojan War and other subjects by artists including Polygnotus.
Zeno of Citium taught there from about 300 BC, and his followers became known as Stoics, "people of the stoa".
American excavators identified foundations of the building in the Agora in 1981.
Athenian public life used the stoa for trials, ceremonies and displays of captured shields.

milestones.text: American School excavations in the Agora find part of the building.

summary: Painted colonnade in the Athenian Agora where Zeno of Citium taught, and from which Stoicism takes its name.
significance: The stoa was a civic monument to Athenian memory that gave its name to one of antiquity's most influential schools.
body:
The Stoa Poikile stood on the north side of the Agora, facing the marketplace. It was built around 460 BC, in the time of Cimon, and was decorated with large paintings on wood panels. Pausanias, who saw them in the second century AD, lists four scenes: the Athenians and Spartans at Oenoe, the Athenians against the Amazons, the aftermath of the fall of Troy, and the battle of Marathon. Polygnotus and Mikon are named as painters.

It was a public building, used for meetings, trials and displays. Captured shields, including some from the Spartans at Sphacteria, were hung in it. Vendors, jugglers and beggars gathered under the roof. Around 300 BC, Zeno of Citium, a Phoenician from Cyprus, began to teach there. His hearers were first called Zenonians, and then Stoics, from the place.

For more than a century the stoa's foundations were not identified. Excavations by the American School in 1981 located part of the building, and confirmed the outline of a long colonnade with an inner wall that could hold panels. The paintings themselves are lost, and the stoa seems to have been dismantled in late antiquity.

That a Stoic philosophy came out of a building of Athenian public memory reflects the kind of school it was. Stoicism taught that a person is part of a rational community, and its meeting-place was a public space, not a private garden or an enclosed grove.

name: The Garden of Epicurus

claims.text: Epicurus founded his school at Athens about 306 BC, in a house and a garden.
The community included women and slaves, which was unusual for a Greek philosophical school.
Members were expected to live simply, share friendship and study the master's teaching.
The location of the Garden itself has not been identified.
Epicurus's will provided for the garden to continue as the school's home after his death.

summary: The house and garden in Athens where Epicurus taught a community of friends, women and slaves included.
significance: The Garden shows philosophy as a way of life lived in a community, and not as a public lecture series.
body:
Epicurus moved to Athens in 307/6 BC and set up his school in a house with a garden, which the Greeks called a kepos. The Garden gave the school its name, and its members were called "those from the Garden". According to Diogenes Laertius, Epicurus bought the property for eighty minas, and he lived there until his death in 270 BC.

The school stood apart from others in Athens. The Academy and Lyceum met in public gymnasia and the Stoa in a civic colonnade, but the Epicureans lived together in a private community. Epicurus's students and friends, including women such as Leontion and slaves such as Mys, shared meals and studied his writings. They aimed at tranquillity, and tried to live without fear of the gods or of death, in the company of friends. A monthly feast celebrated the founder.

The Garden was a household as well as a school, and Epicurus's will, quoted by Diogenes Laertius, provided for its upkeep by his heirs and its use by his followers. The house remained a meeting place for Epicureans for centuries, with a succession of heads, and students such as Lucretius and Philodemus carried its doctrines to Rome.

The precise location of the garden is unknown. Ancient sources suggest that it was between the city and the Academy, and the house was said to be in the deme of Melite. No building or inscription has been securely identified as the school's, and the coordinates given here are only a rough indication of the district.

name: The Acropolis of Athens

claims.text: The Acropolis held a Mycenaean palace and fortification wall in the 13th century BC.
The Persians sacked the Acropolis in 480 BC.
Its main Classical buildings were constructed between 447 and 406 BC.
A gunpowder explosion during the Venetian siege of 1687 wrecked the Parthenon.

milestones.text: Panagiotis Kavvadias excavates the rock down to bedrock, recovering the Archaic statues buried after the Persian sack.
The Committee for the Conservation of the Acropolis Monuments begins the restoration work that continues today.
The new Acropolis Museum opens at the foot of the rock, housing its sculptures.

summary: The rocky citadel at the heart of Athens, crowned by the Parthenon and the other temples of Athena built under Pericles.
significance: The most famous ancient site in the world and the symbol of Classical Greek civilisation and of Athenian democracy at its height.
body:
The Acropolis is a flat-topped limestone hill rising about 70 m above Athens. In the Bronze Age it held a Mycenaean palace, defended by massive walls built in the 13th century BC. Later it became the city's main sanctuary, dedicated above all to Athena, its patron goddess, though it remained a fortress too.

In the Archaic period wealthy Athenians filled it with temples and statues, including the marble korai. When the Persians took Athens in 480 BC they burned the Acropolis. The Athenians buried the damaged statues in the rubble — which is why so many survived — and for a generation left the ruined temples as a memorial.

From 447 BC Pericles rebuilt it on a grand scale, paid for largely by tribute from the Delian League. The Parthenon (447–432 BC) housed Pheidias' gold-and-ivory statue of Athena; the Propylaia (437–432 BC) formed a monumental gateway; the small temple of Athena Nike stood on the bastion beside it; and the Erechtheion (421–406 BC), with its porch of Caryatids, housed the oldest and holiest cults. The great Panathenaic procession climbed to the Acropolis every four years.

The buildings later served as churches, a mosque and an Ottoman fortress. In 1687 a Venetian shell ignited gunpowder stored in the Parthenon, blowing out its centre, and between 1801 and 1812 Lord Elgin removed many sculptures. Restoration has continued since 1975, and the site has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1987.

name: The Parthenon

claims.text: The Parthenon was built between 447 and 432 BC to designs by Iktinos and Kallikrates, with sculpture under Pheidias.
It is a Doric temple of 8 by 17 columns, about 69.5 by 30.9 m at the top step.
It housed Pheidias' gold-and-ivory statue of Athena Parthenos, about 12 m tall.
The building later served as a church and a mosque.

milestones.text: A Venetian shell ignites gunpowder stored inside, blowing out the centre of the building.
Agents of Lord Elgin remove much of the surviving sculpture, now in the British Museum.
A long programme of scientific restoration begins.

summary: The temple of Athena Parthenos on the Acropolis of Athens, built 447–432 BC — the masterpiece of Classical Greek architecture.
significance: The most celebrated building of the ancient world, embodying Athens at the height of its power and the ideals of Classical art.
body:
The Parthenon is the temple of Athena Parthenos ("the Virgin") on the Acropolis of Athens. It was built between 447 and 432 BC as the centrepiece of Pericles' rebuilding programme, on the site of an unfinished temple burned by the Persians in 480 BC. Its architects were Iktinos and Kallikrates, and the sculptor Pheidias directed its decoration. It was paid for largely from the tribute of Athens' allies.

It is a Doric temple of white Pentelic marble, with 8 columns across the ends and 17 along the sides, about 69.5 by 30.9 m. Inside stood Pheidias' statue of Athena, about 12 m tall, of gold and ivory over a wooden core; it is lost. The building is famous for its refinements: the platform curves upward, the columns lean slightly inward and swell along their height, and almost no line is truly straight.

Its sculptures were the most ambitious of any Greek temple: 92 metopes showing mythical battles, a continuous frieze 160 m long of a great procession, and pediments showing the birth of Athena and her contest with Poseidon for Athens. All were brightly painted.

The Parthenon became a church, then a mosque. In 1687, during a Venetian siege, gunpowder stored inside exploded, destroying its centre. Between 1801 and 1812 Lord Elgin removed many sculptures, now in the British Museum, whose return Greece seeks. The rest are in the Acropolis Museum.

name: The Erechtheion

claims.text: The Erechtheion was built between about 421 and 406 BC.
It housed the ancient olive-wood statue of Athena Polias, the holiest image in Athens.
Its south porch is supported by six marble maidens, the Caryatids.
Building accounts inscribed on stone record the wages of citizen, metic and slave workers.

summary: An irregular Ionic temple on the Acropolis, housing Athens' holiest cults and famous for its porch of Caryatids.
significance: The religious heart of the Acropolis, and the source of the Caryatids, among the most copied figures in architecture.
body:
The Erechtheion stands on the north side of the Acropolis, opposite the Parthenon. It was built between about 421 and 406 BC, partly during the Peloponnesian War, and housed the oldest and most sacred cults of Athens: above all the ancient olive-wood statue of Athena Polias, guardian of the city, which received the new robe at the Panathenaia. It also honoured Poseidon and the legendary king Erechtheus, after whom it is named.

Unlike the Parthenon, it is irregular in plan, built across uneven ground and around sacred spots: the marks left by Poseidon's trident when he struck the rock, and Athena's olive tree, her gift that won her the city in the contest with Poseidon. It is in the Ionic order, with finely carved decoration, and has porches on three sides.

The most famous is the south porch, whose roof is held up by six statues of young women, the Caryatids, instead of columns. One was removed by Lord Elgin and is in the British Museum; the others were replaced by copies in the 1970s and are now in the Acropolis Museum.

Inscriptions record the building accounts in detail, listing the wages of the citizens, resident foreigners and slaves who worked side by side, each paid the same daily rate. The temple was later a church, a palace and, under the Ottomans, a harem.

name: The Agora of Athens

claims.text: The Agora was the political, commercial and social centre of ancient Athens.
The American School of Classical Studies has excavated the Agora since 1931.
Over a thousand ostraka and a kleroterion, a machine for selecting citizens by lot, were found there.
The Stoa of Attalos was rebuilt in 1953–56 as the excavation museum.

milestones.text: The American School of Classical Studies at Athens begins excavating the Agora.
The Stoa of Attalos is rebuilt as the Agora Museum.

summary: The great open square of ancient Athens, where citizens met to do business, run the democracy, worship and talk.
significance: The everyday heart of Athenian democracy — and the best-excavated civic centre of any Greek city.
body:
The Agora was the main public square of ancient Athens, an open space north-west of the Acropolis laid out by the 6th century BC. It was surrounded and filled over the centuries by public buildings: the council house (*bouleuterion*) for the Council of 500; the round *tholos* where its standing committee ate and slept; law courts; offices of the magistrates; temples, such as the well-preserved Temple of Hephaestus on the hill above; and long colonnaded halls (*stoas*) such as the Painted Stoa, where Zeno taught and gave the Stoics their name. The Panathenaic Way, the route of the great procession, crossed it to the Acropolis.

It was also a marketplace, full of stalls, workshops and moneychangers, and a place to meet and argue. Socrates spent his days questioning people there.

The American School of Classical Studies at Athens has excavated the Agora since 1931, clearing a whole modern neighbourhood. The finds give a vivid picture of how the democracy worked: ostraka from ostracism votes, a *klērotērion* (allotment machine) for picking jurors at random, bronze juror's tickets, official weights and measures, and a water clock for timing speeches in court. In 1953–56 the Hellenistic Stoa of Attalos, a gift of King Attalos II of Pergamon, was rebuilt as the Agora Museum.

name: Piraeus and the Long Walls

claims.text: Themistocles began fortifying Piraeus as Athens' harbour around 493 BC.
Piraeus was laid out on a grid plan attributed to Hippodamus of Miletus.
The Long Walls linked Athens to the sea in the mid-5th century BC.
Sparta forced Athens to demolish the Long Walls in 404 BC; Conon rebuilt them in the 390s.

summary: The fortified harbour town of Athens, joined to the city by the Long Walls — the base of Athenian sea power.
significance: Piraeus and the Long Walls made Athens effectively an island, able to survive any siege by land as long as it ruled the sea.
body:
Piraeus is a rocky peninsula about 7 km south-west of Athens with three natural harbours: Kantharos, the main commercial port, and Zea and Mounychia, used for warships. Around 493 BC Themistocles began to fortify it as Athens' port in place of the open beach at Phaleron. In the 5th century BC it was laid out as a planned town on a grid of streets, a design credited to Hippodamus of Miletus. It held the shipsheds that housed hundreds of triremes, the grain market and a cosmopolitan population of traders, resident foreigners and sailors.

In the mid-5th century BC the Athenians built the Long Walls, two parallel walls some 6 km long linking Athens to Piraeus, with a third wall to Phaleron. They turned the city and its harbour into a single fortress. In the Peloponnesian War, Pericles relied on them: the people of Attica moved inside, and Athens was supplied by sea while Spartan armies ravaged the countryside. The crowding also helped spread the plague of 430 BC, which entered through the port.

When Athens surrendered in 404 BC, Sparta forced it to pull down the Long Walls to the music of flute-girls. The Athenian general Conon rebuilt them in the 390s with Persian money. Sulla destroyed the port's fortifications in 86 BC. Piraeus remains Greece's largest port.

name: The Temple of Artemis at Ephesus

claims.text: The Archaic temple of Artemis was built from around 560 BC with funding from King Croesus of Lydia.
It was burned in 356 BC by Herostratus, who sought fame by the act.
The rebuilt temple was counted among the Seven Wonders of the ancient world.
A foundation deposit at the temple contained some of the earliest known coins.

milestones.text: John Turtle Wood, digging for the British Museum, finds the temple's remains under metres of silt.
David Hogarth finds the foundation deposit with the earliest dated coins.

summary: The vast Ionic temple of Artemis at Ephesus, one of the largest Greek temples ever built and one of the Seven Wonders of the ancient world.
significance: A Wonder of the ancient world and a meeting point of Greek and Anatolian religion; its foundation deposit preserves the earliest dated coins.
body:
The sanctuary of Artemis at Ephesus, on the coast of Ionia in western Asia Minor, was among the most important in the Greek world. Its goddess, Artemis of Ephesus, combined the Greek huntress with an older Anatolian mother goddess.

Around 560 BC the Ephesians began a huge marble temple in the Ionic order, about 115 by 55 m, surrounded by a double row of columns, more than a hundred in all. King Croesus of Lydia paid for many of its columns. It was one of the first great marble temples and one of the largest Greek temples ever built.

In 356 BC a man named Herostratus burned it down to make his name famous; the Ephesians decreed his name should never be spoken. Later tradition said the fire happened on the night Alexander the Great was born. The Ephesians rebuilt it on the same plan, refusing Alexander's offer to pay for it, and the new temple was listed among the Seven Wonders of the ancient world.

It was damaged by Gothic raiders in the AD 260s and its stone was later reused. Its site, buried by silt, was found in 1869 by John Turtle Wood. Beneath the temple, David Hogarth in 1904–05 found a foundation deposit of electrum coins, among the earliest known. Today a single re-erected column marks the spot.

name: The Mausoleum of Halicarnassus

claims.text: The Mausoleum was built for Mausolus, ruler of Caria, who died in 353 BC, and completed under his wife Artemisia II.
Leading Greek sculptors including Scopas worked on its sculpture.
The Knights of St John reused its stones to build their castle at Bodrum, completing the work by 1494.
Charles Newton excavated its remains in 1856–57.

milestones.text: Its ruins, already brought down by earthquakes, are quarried by the Knights of St John for Bodrum Castle.
Charles Newton excavates the site and ships sculptures to the British Museum.

summary: The monumental tomb of Mausolus, ruler of Caria, built in the 350s BC — one of the Seven Wonders and the origin of the word "mausoleum".
significance: A meeting of Greek and Persian-world art, decorated by the leading Greek sculptors of the 4th century BC, which gave its name to every later mausoleum.
body:
Mausolus ruled Caria, in south-western Asia Minor, as a satrap of the Persian king, but in practice as an independent prince. He made Halicarnassus (modern Bodrum) his capital and began a vast tomb for himself there. After his death in 353 BC his widow and sister, Artemisia II, continued the work.

The Mausoleum stood about 45 m tall. A high rectangular base supported a colonnade of Ionic columns, topped by a stepped pyramid roof crowned with a marble four-horse chariot. Its architects were Pytheos and Satyros, and according to Pliny four of the most famous Greek sculptors — Scopas, Bryaxis, Timotheus and Leochares — each carved one side. Friezes showed battles of Greeks and Amazons and of Lapiths and centaurs, and there were many free-standing statues. It mixed Greek, Egyptian and Near Eastern elements and was counted among the Seven Wonders of the ancient world.

It stood for many centuries until damaged by earthquakes in the Middle Ages. The Knights of St John then used its stones to build their castle at Bodrum, finishing by 1494. In 1856–57 the British archaeologist Charles Newton excavated the site and took sculptures, including the great statues long identified as Mausolus and Artemisia, to the British Museum.

The name of Mausolus became the general word for a grand tomb.

name: The Pharos of Alexandria

claims.text: The lighthouse was completed around 280 BC under Ptolemy II, designed by Sostratus of Cnidus.
It stood about 100 m tall, among the tallest structures of the ancient world.
Earthquakes in the 14th century AD brought it down.
Blocks from the lighthouse have been found on the seabed of Alexandria's harbour since 1994.

milestones.text: After centuries of earthquake damage, the last of the tower collapses.
Sultan Qaitbay builds a fort on its site, reusing its stone.
Divers led by Jean-Yves Empereur begin mapping its fallen blocks and statues in the harbour.

summary: The great lighthouse at the entrance to Alexandria's harbour, completed around 280 BC — one of the Seven Wonders of the ancient world.
significance: The prototype of every lighthouse: its name, pharos, still means lighthouse in many languages, and it guided ships into the greatest port of the Hellenistic world for 1,500 years.
body:
The Pharos stood on the eastern tip of the island of Pharos, which a causeway linked to the mainland at Alexandria, the capital of Ptolemaic Egypt. It was begun under Ptolemy I and completed around 280 BC under Ptolemy II. Its architect was Sostratus of Cnidus, whose dedication to the "Saviour Gods" was inscribed on it.

Ancient and medieval descriptions agree that it rose in three tiers: a square base, an octagonal middle and a round top, crowned by a statue, probably of Zeus. It stood perhaps 100 m tall, among the tallest structures of the ancient world. A fire burned at the top, and some sources say a mirror reflected its light out to sea. It guided ships along a flat, dangerous coast into one of the busiest ports of the Mediterranean, and was counted among the Seven Wonders. Its name became the word for lighthouse in Greek, Latin and many later languages, such as French *phare* and Italian *faro*.

The Pharos survived for some 1,500 years, repaired many times, until earthquakes in the 14th century AD brought it down. In 1477 the Mamluk sultan Qaitbay built a fort on its site, reusing some of its stone. Since 1994 underwater archaeologists led by Jean-Yves Empereur have found huge blocks, columns and colossal statues of the Ptolemies on the seabed nearby.

name: The Treasury of Atreus

claims.text: The Treasury of Atreus is a Mycenaean tholos tomb built around 1250 BC.
Its corbelled dome is about 13.5 m high and 14.5 m across.
The inner lintel over its doorway weighs an estimated 120 tonnes.
Its links to Atreus and Agamemnon are later legend.

summary: The grandest Mycenaean beehive tomb, built around 1250 BC outside Mycenae, whose stone dome stayed the largest in the world for over a thousand years.
significance: The supreme achievement of Mycenaean architecture and engineering, and the clearest sign of the wealth and power of Mycenae's kings.
body:
The Treasury of Atreus is a *tholos*, or beehive tomb, cut into a hillside just outside the citadel of Mycenae in the Argolid, and built around 1250 BC. Pausanias, who saw it in the 2nd century AD, repeated the local belief that it was the treasury of Atreus, father of Agamemnon; it is also called the Tomb of Agamemnon. Both names are legend; whose tomb it was is unknown, and it was robbed long ago.

A passage (*dromos*) 36 m long, lined with fine masonry, leads to a doorway more than 5 m high. Above it, a triangular opening relieves the weight on the lintel — the same device used over the Lion Gate. The inner lintel is a single block estimated at about 120 tonnes. The façade was once decorated with columns and carved stone panels of green and red stone, some now in the British Museum.

Inside, a round chamber is roofed by a corbelled dome, built of 33 rings of stone blocks, each ring projecting slightly inward over the one below, about 13.5 m high and 14.5 m across. It was the largest dome in the world until Roman times. A small side chamber cut into the rock probably held the burials.

The Treasury of Atreus and the other tholos tombs at Mycenae show the immense resources Mycenaean rulers could command at the height of their power.

name: Carthage

claims.text: Carthage was founded by Phoenicians from Tyre, traditionally in 814 BC.
Carthage fought the Sicilian Greeks for over two centuries.
Rome destroyed Carthage in 146 BC, the same year it sacked Corinth.

summary: The great Phoenician city of North Africa, rival of the western Greeks and of Rome, destroyed in 146 BC.
significance: The main rival of the Greeks in the western Mediterranean for three centuries, and of Rome in the Punic Wars.
body:
Carthage stood on a peninsula on the coast of North Africa, near modern Tunis. Phoenicians from Tyre founded it, traditionally in 814 BC; the oldest archaeological remains date to the later 9th or 8th century BC. It grew into the leading Phoenician city of the west, with a powerful navy and a trading network across the western Mediterranean, from Sardinia and Spain to the Atlantic coast.

Its expansion brought it into conflict with the Greek colonies. In the 6th century BC it fought the Phocaeans at sea off Alalia in Corsica. In Sicily, Carthaginians and Greeks fought for control of the island for over two centuries: Gelon of Syracuse defeated a Carthaginian army at Himera in 480 BC, by tradition on the same day as Salamis; Carthage destroyed Selinous and Akragas in 409–406 BC; and wars continued under Dionysius I, Timoleon and Agathocles, who invaded Africa itself in 310 BC.

Carthage was governed by a mercantile aristocracy with elected magistrates, the *suffetes*, and a council; Aristotle praised its constitution. Its gods included Baal Hammon and Tanit.

Its rivalry with Rome led to the three Punic Wars (264–146 BC), including Hannibal's invasion of Italy. At the end of the Third Punic War, in 146 BC, Rome destroyed Carthage, the same year it sacked Corinth.

name: Sardis

claims.text: Sardis was the capital of the kingdom of Lydia.
Gold refineries of the 6th century BC have been excavated at Sardis.
Cyrus captured Sardis around 546 BC, ending the Lydian kingdom.
Rebels in the Ionian Revolt burned Sardis in 498 BC.

milestones.text: Harvard and Cornell begin the Archaeological Exploration of Sardis, which continues today.

summary: The capital of the kingdom of Lydia in western Asia Minor, city of Croesus and birthplace of coinage, and later a Persian provincial capital.
significance: The rich Lydian capital where coinage began, whose fall to Persia brought the Persian Empire into contact with the Greeks.
body:
Sardis lay in the valley of the river Hermus in western Asia Minor, below a steep acropolis. It was the capital of the kingdom of Lydia, which under the Mermnad dynasty of the 7th and 6th centuries BC dominated western Anatolia and the Greek cities of Ionia. Its wealth came partly from the gold in the Pactolus river, which flowed through the city. Excavations have uncovered the workshops where Lydians refined gold and silver, and it was in Lydia, in the late 7th century BC, that the first coins were struck.

Sardis was the city of King Croesus, whose wealth was legendary. Around 546 BC Cyrus the Great captured it, ending the Lydian kingdom, and it became the capital of the Persian province of Lydia and the western end of the Royal Road to Susa. In 498 BC Ionian rebels, with Athenian help, burned the city, an act Persia remembered when it invaded Greece.

Alexander took Sardis without a fight in 334 BC. Under the Seleucids and Romans it remained an important city; the great temple of Artemis was built in the Hellenistic period, and in Roman times it had one of the largest synagogues of the ancient world.

The Archaeological Exploration of Sardis, led by Harvard and Cornell, has excavated the city since 1958.

name: Franchthi Cave

milestones.text: Thomas W. Jacobsen of Indiana University begins excavation, continuing until 1979

claims.text: Franchthi Cave was used by people, on and off, from about 38,000 BC to about 3000 BC.
Obsidian from the island of Melos appears in its levels from around 11,000 BC, the earliest evidence of seafaring in the Aegean.
The cave records the change from hunting and gathering to farming, which appears there around 7000 BC.

summary: A cave on the coast of the Argolid used for over 30,000 years, whose deposits trace the change from hunting to farming in Greece.
significance: The longest sequence of prehistoric occupation in Greece, and the earliest evidence of sea travel in the Aegean.
body:
Franchthi Cave lies on a bay of the southern Argolid, opposite the village of Kilada. It was excavated from 1967 to 1979 by Thomas W. Jacobsen of Indiana University, and its deposits, many metres deep, revealed a history of use stretching from about 38,000 BC, in the Upper Palaeolithic, to the end of the Neolithic around 3000 BC.

In the Ice Age, when the sea was much lower, the cave looked out over a coastal plain. Its early inhabitants hunted wild horse, deer and wild cattle. Around 11,000 BC flakes of obsidian, a volcanic glass, appear; analysis has shown it came from the island of Melos, more than 100 kilometres away across open sea, so these hunter-gatherers must have travelled by boat. In the Mesolithic, after about 8000 BC, the people of Franchthi caught large fish such as tuna.

Around 7000 BC domesticated sheep and goats, wheat, barley and lentils appear, along with pottery soon afterwards — part of the arrival of farming in Greece. A farming village grew up on the shore in front of the cave, now partly under the sea. Burials, including that of a young man of the Mesolithic, were found inside the cave.

name: Sesklo

milestones.text: Christos Tsountas excavates the Neolithic settlement
Dimitrios Theocharis begins new excavations, continuing to 1977

claims.text: Sesklo was one of the largest Neolithic villages in Greece, occupied from the early 7th millennium BC.
It gives its name to the Middle Neolithic Sesklo culture of Thessaly, known for red-on-white painted pottery.
Estimates of its population at its height, ranging from a few hundred to several thousand, are disputed.

summary: A large Neolithic village in Thessaly, occupied from about 6800 BC, which gives its name to the Middle Neolithic culture of the region.
significance: One of the earliest and largest farming villages in Europe.
body:
Sesklo lies in the hills west of Volos, in the fertile plain of Thessaly, which had the densest population of Neolithic Greece. It was excavated by Christos Tsountas in 1901–02 and again by Dimitrios Theocharis between 1956 and 1977.

The settlement began early in the Neolithic, around 6800 BC, and grew into one of the largest villages of its time. It had two parts: a small hill, the "acropolis", with closely packed houses, and a much larger surrounding settlement. The houses had stone foundations and walls of mudbrick or wattle and daub, and some were two-storeyed. A larger building on the hilltop has been interpreted as a chief's house or a communal hall. How many people lived there at its height is disputed, with estimates ranging from a few hundred to several thousand.

The villagers grew wheat, barley and pulses and kept sheep and goats. Sesklo gives its name to the Middle Neolithic culture of Thessaly (c. 6000–5300 BC), known for fine pottery painted with red geometric patterns on a white surface, and for clay figurines. Parts of the settlement were burned around the middle of the 6th millennium, and in the Late Neolithic the nearby village of Dimini became more important.

name: Dimini

milestones.text: Christos Tsountas begins excavating the Neolithic settlement, after Valerios Stais found a Mycenaean tholos tomb there in 1886

claims.text: Dimini was a Late Neolithic village of about 4800–4500 BC enclosed by a series of concentric stone walls.
The walls are now usually seen as enclosures dividing households rather than fortifications.
The site was reoccupied in the Mycenaean period, when tholos tombs and a settlement were built nearby.

summary: A Late Neolithic village near Volos in Thessaly, of about 4800–4500 BC, surrounded by concentric stone walls.
significance: The best-known Neolithic settlement in Greece, and the type site of the Late Neolithic Dimini culture.
body:
Dimini stands on a low hill a few kilometres from Sesklo, near the shore of the Pagasetic Gulf at Volos. In 1886 Valerios Stais found a Mycenaean tholos tomb nearby, and from 1901 Christos Tsountas excavated the Neolithic village on the hilltop. Later excavations have continued there.

The village was occupied mainly in the Late Neolithic, around 4800–4500 BC. Its most striking feature is a series of up to six low stone walls running in rough rings around the hill, with narrow passages between them. Early excavators took these for fortifications, but they are too low and too many to be defensive, and are now usually seen as enclosures dividing groups of houses and work areas. At the centre was a courtyard with a larger house, once compared to the Mycenaean megaron. Excavators found hearths, storage pits, and evidence of pottery-making and shell-working.

Dimini gives its name to the Late Neolithic culture of Thessaly, known for pottery decorated with spirals and meanders in dark paint. Long after the village was abandoned, the site was reoccupied in the Mycenaean period, when a settlement and two tholos tombs were built; some scholars identify it with ancient Iolcos.

name: Serapeum of Alexandria

milestones.text: Alan Rowe's excavations find the bilingual foundation plaques of Ptolemy III

claims.text: The Serapeum was built by Ptolemy III, as foundation plaques in Greek and Egyptian show.
It housed a 'daughter' library of the great Library of Alexandria.
It was destroyed by Christians in AD 391.

relations.rel: held branch of library founded in

summary: The great temple of Serapis in Alexandria, built by Ptolemy III around 240 BC and destroyed by Christians in AD 391.
significance: The religious heart of Greek Alexandria and home of a second library, whose destruction in 391 marked the end of the pagan city.
body:
The Serapeum stood on a rocky hill in the south-west of Alexandria, in the old Egyptian quarter of Rhakotis. A smaller shrine of Serapis may have existed there under the first Ptolemies, but the great temple was built by Ptolemy III, as shown by foundation plaques in Greek and hieroglyphs found in the excavations of Alan Rowe in the 1940s. It was rebuilt on a larger scale by the Romans in the 2nd century AD.

The temple housed a famous cult statue of Serapis, enthroned and bearded like Zeus, with the three-headed dog Cerberus beside him; ancient writers attributed it to the sculptor Bryaxis. Around it were colonnades, and rooms that held a "daughter" library, open more widely than the main Library in the palace quarter. Beneath the temple ran underground galleries, perhaps for the burial of sacred animals.

In AD 391, after the emperor Theodosius I banned pagan sacrifice, the bishop Theophilus led Christians in destroying the temple and its statue, a moment Christian writers celebrated as the triumph of the new faith. A great granite column set up for the emperor Diocletian in AD 297, misnamed "Pompey's Pillar", still stands on the site.

name: Nicopolis

claims.text: Octavian founded Nicopolis, "Victory City", on the site of his camp after the battle of Actium in 31 BC.
He filled it by moving the populations of surrounding towns and founded the Actian Games there.
The philosopher Epictetus taught at Nicopolis in the late 1st and early 2nd centuries AD.

summary: The "Victory City" founded by Octavian in north-western Greece to celebrate his victory at Actium in 31 BC.
significance: The largest Roman foundation in Greece, a monument to the battle that ended the Hellenistic age, and later the home of Epictetus' school.
body:
Nicopolis stands on the isthmus north of the Ambracian Gulf, opposite Actium, where Octavian camped before defeating Antony and Cleopatra in 31 BC. Soon afterwards he founded a city on the site of his camp and named it Nicopolis, "Victory City". He populated it by moving, often by force, the inhabitants of many towns of Epirus, Acarnania and Aetolia, and made it a free city with a vote in the Amphictyonic Council of Delphi.

On the hill where his tent had stood he built a victory monument decorated with the bronze rams of captured warships; the sockets for them can still be seen. He also refounded the Actian Games, held every four years in honour of Apollo, which ranked with the Olympic Games.

Nicopolis became the main city of north-western Greece. The Stoic Epictetus taught there from the 90s AD, and Paul wrote of planning to spend a winter there. The city had a theatre, an odeon, a stadium, baths and an aqueduct; in the early Christian period it was a bishop's seat with large mosaic-floored basilicas. It declined after raids in the early Middle Ages and was abandoned by the 11th century. Its walls and ruins survive.

name: Temple of Olympian Zeus, Athens

claims.text: Work on the temple began around 520 BC under the sons of Peisistratus and stopped when the tyranny fell.
Antiochus IV resumed it in 174 BC with the Roman architect Cossutius, in the Corinthian order.
Hadrian completed and dedicated it in AD 131/2, about 650 years after it was begun.

summary: The colossal temple of Zeus in Athens, begun around 520 BC and finished by Hadrian in AD 131/2.
significance: One of the largest temples of the ancient world, whose six-century construction spans the whole history of Athens from tyranny to Roman empire.
body:
The temple stands south-east of the Acropolis, on the site of an older sanctuary of Zeus. Around 520 BC the sons of the tyrant Peisistratus began a vast limestone temple, meant to rival the great temples of Samos and Ephesus. When the tyranny fell in 510 BC the work was abandoned, and later Athenians saw the unfinished foundations as a monument to tyrants' arrogance.

In 174 BC the Seleucid king Antiochus IV paid to resume it, employing a Roman architect, Cossutius, who redesigned it in marble in the new Corinthian order. Work stopped again at the king's death. According to Pliny, when Sulla sacked Athens in 86 BC he carried some of its columns off to Rome for the temple of Jupiter on the Capitol.

The temple was finally completed by Hadrian, who dedicated it in AD 131/2. With 104 Corinthian columns about 17 metres high, it was among the largest temples in the Greek world. It housed a gold-and-ivory statue of Zeus and a statue of Hadrian himself. Probably damaged in the Herulian raid of 267, it was later quarried for stone. Fifteen columns still stand; a sixteenth was blown down in a storm in 1852 and lies where it fell.

name: Library of Hadrian

claims.text: Hadrian built the library in Athens in AD 132.
Pausanias describes it as having a hundred columns, with rooms decorated with gilded ceilings and alabaster.
It was damaged in the Herulian sack of AD 267 and later incorporated into the city's defences.

summary: The great library and colonnaded court built by Hadrian in the centre of Athens in AD 132.
significance: The grandest of Hadrian's gifts to Athens, combining a library, lecture halls and a garden court.
body:
The Library of Hadrian lies north of the Acropolis, beside the Roman Agora. It was a large rectangular enclosure, about 122 by 82 metres, entered through a monumental gateway with columns of green-veined marble on its west side. Inside, a colonnaded court with a long pool and garden surrounded the main buildings. Pausanias, who saw it a generation later, counted a hundred columns.

On the east side was the library itself: a central hall with niches in its walls for wooden bookcases holding papyrus rolls, flanked by reading or lecture rooms and rooms at the corners that may have served as small auditoria. The complex was probably also used for public archives and as a place for teaching.

The library was damaged when the Heruli sacked Athens in AD 267, and its walls were then built into the late Roman defences. It was restored around 410 by a Roman prefect, and in the 5th century a church was built in the court; it was rebuilt several times over the following centuries. Part of its west façade, with its Corinthian columns, still stands on Areos Street in the Monastiraki district.

name: Odeon of Herodes Atticus

milestones.text: Seating restored in marble; the theatre becomes the main stage of the Athens Festival

claims.text: Herodes Atticus built the Odeon on the south slope of the Acropolis in memory of his wife Regilla, who died in AD 160.
It seated about 5,000 people and had a roof of cedar wood.
Restored in the 1950s, it is still used for concerts and plays.

summary: The roofed theatre built by Herodes Atticus on the south slope of the Acropolis after AD 160, still used for performances.
significance: The best-preserved ancient theatre in Athens and a living stage for the Athens Festival.
body:
The Odeon stands on the south-west slope of the Acropolis, west of the much older Theatre of Dionysus. Herodes Atticus built it after the death of his wife Regilla in 160 as a memorial to her. Pausanias, writing in the 170s, calls it the finest odeon in Greece and says it had a roof of cedar wood — an extraordinary span for a building of its size, though some scholars doubt the whole auditorium was covered.

An *odeon* was a hall for music, recitations and speeches, smaller and more intimate than an open-air theatre. Herodes' Odeon had a steep semicircular auditorium cut into the hillside, seating about 5,000, and a three-storey stone stage building with arched windows, whose tall façade still survives. The floor of the orchestra was paved with black and white marble.

The Odeon was probably destroyed when the Heruli sacked Athens in 267. Its ruins were later built into fortifications. In the 1950s the seating was restored in marble, and since then the Odeon has been the main stage of the Athens Festival, hosting ancient drama, opera and concerts.

name: Oxyrhynchus

milestones.text: Bernard Grenfell and Arthur Hunt begin digging the town's rubbish mounds, continuing to 1907
First volume of The Oxyrhynchus Papyri, a series still continuing

claims.text: The rubbish mounds of Oxyrhynchus have produced more Greek papyri than any other site.
Grenfell and Hunt excavated there between 1896 and 1907.
The papyri include lost works of Sappho, Pindar, Menander and others, and some of the earliest fragments of Christian texts.

summary: A Graeco-Roman town in Middle Egypt whose rubbish dumps yielded the largest find of Greek papyri ever made.
significance: The richest single source of lost Greek literature and of everyday life in Roman Egypt.
body:
Oxyrhynchus, "town of the sharp-nosed fish", named after a fish sacred to the local Egyptians, lay on a canal west of the Nile about 160 kilometres south of Cairo, at modern el-Bahnasa. Under the Ptolemies and the Romans it was a prosperous provincial capital with Greek-speaking officials, a theatre for some 11,000 spectators, temples, and later churches and monasteries.

For a thousand years its people threw old papers — tax returns, letters, school exercises, worn-out books — onto rubbish mounds at the edge of the desert, where the dry sand preserved them. In 1896 two young Oxford scholars, Bernard Grenfell and Arthur Hunt, began digging the mounds, and over eleven seasons recovered hundreds of thousands of fragments. They began publishing them in 1898 in *The Oxyrhynchus Papyri*, a series that has passed eighty volumes and is still continuing, with much still unread.

Most of the texts are documents of daily life, but the literary finds are extraordinary: poems of Sappho, Alcaeus and Pindar, plays of Menander and Sophocles' satyr play *The Trackers*, lost histories, and early Christian texts including sayings of Jesus later identified as part of the Gospel of Thomas. New techniques such as multispectral imaging are revealing more.

name: Constantinople

claims.text: Constantine refounded the Greek city of Byzantion as Constantinople and dedicated it on 11 May 330.
It was the largest and richest city in Europe for much of the Middle Ages, with perhaps 400,000–500,000 people at its height in the 6th century.
It withstood numerous sieges until the Fourth Crusade took it in 1204, and fell finally to the Ottomans in 1453.

summary: The capital of the Byzantine Empire, founded by Constantine on the Bosporus in AD 330 and taken by the Ottomans in 1453.
significance: For over a thousand years the greatest city of the Christian world, "the city" of the Greeks, where Roman government, Orthodox Christianity and Greek learning were preserved.
body:
Constantinople stood on a triangular peninsula between the Sea of Marmara and the Golden Horn, a deep natural harbour, commanding the Bosporus strait between Europe and Asia. It was built on the site of Byzantion, a Greek colony founded from Megara in the 7th century BC. In 324 Constantine chose it as his new capital and greatly enlarged it, dedicating it on 11 May 330 as a New Rome, with a senate, a hippodrome, palaces and churches.

The city became the largest and richest in Europe. Its walls — above all the land walls of Theodosius II, built in 413 — protected it from Huns, Avars, Persians, Arabs, Bulgars and Rus' for eight centuries. Its monuments included the great church of Hagia Sophia, the Great Palace, the Hippodrome with its obelisk and bronze serpent column brought from Delphi, and markets that drew merchants from across Europe and Asia.

The Greeks often called it simply *hē Polis*, "the City". It was sacked by the Fourth Crusade in 1204 and held by the Latins until 1261, then recovered but impoverished. On 29 May 1453 the Ottoman sultan Mehmed II took it and made it his capital. It is now Istanbul, whose name derives from the Greek phrase *eis tēn polin*, "to the City".

name: Theodosian Walls

claims.text: The land walls were built in 413 under Theodosius II by the prefect Anthemius.
After an earthquake in 447 they were rebuilt in about two months and strengthened with an outer wall and moat.
They were not breached by an enemy army until the Ottoman siege of 1453.

summary: The triple land walls of Constantinople, built in 413 and strengthened in 447, which protected the city for over a thousand years.
significance: The most successful fortifications of the Middle Ages, which saved Constantinople — and arguably Europe — from many invaders.
body:
Constantinople was protected by the sea on two sides, but its western side, facing Thrace, needed strong defences. In 413, under the young emperor Theodosius II, the prefect Anthemius built a new line of walls about 1.5 kilometres west of Constantine's, running some 6 kilometres from the Sea of Marmara to the Golden Horn.

In 447 an earthquake brought down much of the wall just as Attila's Huns approached. The people of the city, organised by the circus factions, rebuilt it in about two months, as an inscription records, and added an outer wall and a broad moat. The result was a triple barrier: a moat about 20 metres wide, an outer wall, and an inner wall about 12 metres high with 96 towers.

The walls defeated Avars and Persians in 626, Arabs in 674–678 and 717–718, and Bulgars and Rus' later. In 1204 the Crusaders entered the city from the sea walls along the Golden Horn, not through the land walls. Only in 1453 did Mehmed II's huge cannon batter breaches in them, and the Ottomans broke through on 29 May. Long stretches, partly restored, still run across Istanbul.

name: Hagia Sophia

milestones.text: Converted into a mosque by Mehmed II after the Ottoman conquest
Made a museum by the Turkish Republic under Atatürk.
Reconverted into a mosque by presidential decree.

claims.text: Justinian's Hagia Sophia was built in under six years, from 532 to 537, by the architects Anthemius of Tralles and Isidore of Miletus.
Its original dome collapsed in 558 and was rebuilt higher in 562.
It was the largest church in the world for nearly a thousand years.

summary: The great church of Constantinople, built by Justinian in 532–537, whose vast dome was the wonder of the medieval world.
significance: The supreme achievement of Byzantine architecture and the cathedral of Orthodox Christianity for nine centuries.
body:
An earlier church of Holy Wisdom (*Hagia Sophia*) on the site was burned in the Nika riots of 532. Justinian immediately ordered a new one, designed not by ordinary builders but by two scientists, Anthemius of Tralles, a mathematician, and Isidore of Miletus, a geometer. With some 10,000 workers it was finished in less than six years and dedicated on 27 December 537; Justinian is said to have exclaimed, "Solomon, I have surpassed you!"

The building combines a long basilica with a huge central dome, about 31 metres across, carried on four great arches and pendentives and buttressed by half-domes. A ring of forty windows at its base makes the dome seem to float; the historian Procopius wrote that it appeared to be hung from heaven by a golden chain. The interior was covered in gold mosaics and coloured marbles. The first dome, too shallow, collapsed after an earthquake in 558 and was rebuilt higher in 562.

Hagia Sophia was the seat of the patriarch and the setting of imperial coronations. After the Ottoman conquest in 1453 it became a mosque, with minarets added; in 1934 it was made a museum, and in 2020 it was turned back into a mosque. Many of its Byzantine mosaics survive.

name: Mount Athos

claims.text: The Great Lavra, the first large monastery on Athos, was founded in 963 by Athanasios the Athonite with the support of Nikephoros Phokas.
Twenty ruling monasteries survive, and the peninsula is a self-governing monastic state within Greece.
Its libraries hold thousands of Byzantine manuscripts.

summary: The mountainous peninsula in northern Greece that has been the centre of Orthodox monasticism since the 10th century.
significance: A living survival of Byzantium, whose monasteries preserve Byzantine art, liturgy and manuscripts.
body:
Mount Athos is the easternmost of the three peninsulas of Chalcidice in northern Greece, ending in a marble peak over 2,000 metres high. In antiquity Xerxes cut a canal across its neck in 480 BC to spare his fleet the dangerous voyage round it. Hermits lived there from at least the 9th century.

In 963 the monk Athanasios, with the support of his friend the general and future emperor Nikephoros II Phokas, founded the Great Lavra, the first large organised monastery. Others followed, founded by Byzantine emperors and later by Georgian, Serbian, Russian and Bulgarian rulers, making Athos a centre for the whole Orthodox world. Imperial charters gave it self-government; by tradition, women and even female animals are barred.

Athos flourished in the late Byzantine period, when it was the home of Hesychasm, a movement of contemplative prayer. After 1430 it submitted to the Ottomans and kept its privileges. Today twenty ruling monasteries remain, governing the peninsula as a self-governing region of Greece; it was made a World Heritage Site in 1988. Its monasteries preserve icons, frescoes, treasures and thousands of manuscripts, including copies of classical texts.

name: Mystras

claims.text: Mystras was founded as a castle in 1249 by the Frankish prince William II of Villehardouin and handed to the Byzantines in 1262.
It became the capital of the Byzantine Despotate of the Morea and a centre of late Byzantine learning.
Constantine XI, the last emperor, was proclaimed there in 1449; it fell to the Ottomans in 1460.

summary: The hillside fortress-city above Sparta that was the capital of Byzantine southern Greece and a last centre of Byzantine culture, until 1460.
significance: Where Byzantine learning, art and the revival of Plato flourished in the empire's last century; its churches and palace survive.
body:
Mystras rises on a steep foothill of Mount Taygetos, about 6 kilometres west of ancient Sparta. In 1249 William II of Villehardouin, the French prince of Achaea who ruled much of the Peloponnese after the Fourth Crusade, built a castle on its summit. Captured by the Byzantines, he handed it over in 1262 as part of his ransom.

A town grew on the slopes beneath the castle, and Mystras became the seat of the Byzantine governors and then, from 1349, of the Despots of the Morea, usually sons or brothers of the emperor. While the empire shrank to Constantinople, the Despotate expanded until it ruled almost all the Peloponnese. Mystras had a palace, monasteries and churches decorated with some of the finest late Byzantine frescoes, such as those of the Peribleptos and the Pantanassa.

It was also an intellectual centre, home to the philosopher Gemistos Plethon, who taught a revived Platonism. In 1449 Constantine XI Palaiologos was proclaimed emperor there before going to Constantinople. Mystras surrendered to the Ottomans in 1460, seven years after the fall of the capital. Abandoned in the 19th century when modern Sparta was built, it is now a World Heritage Site.

name: Thessalonica

claims.text: Cassander founded Thessalonica around 315 BC and named it after his wife, a half-sister of Alexander the Great.
It was the second city of the Byzantine Empire, famed for the cult of its patron saint Demetrios.
It was sacked by Arabs in 904 and Normans in 1185, and taken by the Ottomans in 1430.

summary: The Macedonian port founded by Cassander around 315 BC, which became the second city of the Byzantine Empire.
significance: For over a thousand years the great city of the Greek north, whose churches are among the finest monuments of early and middle Byzantine art.
body:
Thessalonica was founded around 315 BC by Cassander, king of Macedon, who merged some two dozen villages at the head of the Thermaic Gulf and named the city after his wife Thessalonike, half-sister of Alexander the Great. Under Rome it was the capital of the province of Macedonia and a station on the Via Egnatia, the road from the Adriatic to Byzantium. Paul founded one of the first Christian churches in Europe there around AD 50 and wrote it the earliest of his letters.

Around AD 300 the emperor Galerius made it his residence, building a palace, a triumphal arch and a great round building, the Rotunda, later a church. In 390 Theodosius I's soldiers massacred thousands of citizens in the hippodrome.

In the Byzantine period Thessalonica was the empire's second city and the centre of the cult of Saint Demetrios, a soldier-martyr believed to protect it; his great basilica still stands. The brothers Cyril and Methodius, apostles to the Slavs, came from the city.
