It was sacked by Arab raiders in 904 and by the Normans of Sicily in 1185, ruled by a Latin king after 1204, and governed by a radical "Zealot" regime in 1342–50. Ceded to Venice in 1423, it fell to the Ottoman sultan Murad II in 1430.

name: Roman Corinth

claims.text: Julius Caesar refounded Corinth in 44 BC as a Roman colony, a century after its destruction in 146 BC.
Settled largely by freedmen from Italy, it became the capital of the province of Achaea.
Paul spent eighteen months in Corinth around AD 50–52 and wrote two surviving letters to its church.

summary: The Roman colony founded by Julius Caesar on the ruins of Corinth in 44 BC, which became the capital of Roman Greece.
significance: The richest city of Roman Greece, where Paul founded one of the most important early Christian communities.
body:
Rome destroyed Greek Corinth in 146 BC. A century later, in 44 BC, Julius Caesar refounded it as a Roman colony, *Colonia Laus Iulia Corinthiensis*, settled largely with freed slaves from Italy. With its two harbours on the Saronic and Corinthian gulfs and its control of the Isthmus, it quickly grew rich again, and under Augustus it became the seat of the governor of the province of Achaea.

The city was rebuilt on a Roman plan, with Latin as its official language for over a century. Most of the ruins visitors see today are Roman: the great forum, with its speaker's platform (*bema*), basilicas, shops and temples, the Lechaion Road, and the Peirene fountain, rebuilt in marble with help from Herodes Atticus. Only the archaic temple of Apollo survived from the Greek city. The Isthmian Games were brought back under Corinthian control.

Paul arrived around AD 50 and stayed eighteen months, working as a tentmaker; he was accused before the governor Gallio, perhaps at the *bema*. His letters to the Corinthians, written in the 50s, give a vivid picture of the young church there. The city was damaged by earthquakes in the 4th century and sacked by the Goths under Alaric in 396.

name: Propylaea

claims.text: The Propylaea, the gateway to the Acropolis, was built in 437–432 BC to the design of Mnesicles.
It combines Doric outer façades with Ionic columns in the central passage.
It was never finished; work stopped on the eve of the Peloponnesian War.

milestones.text: A gunpowder store inside explodes after a lightning strike, wrecking the central hall

summary: The marble gateway to the Acropolis of Athens, built by Mnesicles in 437–432 BC and never completed.
significance: The grandest entrance building of classical Greece and a key part of Pericles' Acropolis.
body:
After the Parthenon, Pericles' programme turned to a new entrance for the Acropolis, replacing an older gateway damaged by the Persians. Mnesicles' Propylaea was built of Pentelic marble from 437 to 432 BC. Its accounts, inscribed on stone, record a cost of over 2,000 talents for the whole building, though the figure is debated.

The central building had a Doric portico of six columns facing west, a passage flanked by Ionic columns rising up the slope, and a wall pierced by five doors, the central one wide enough for sacrificial animals and the chariots of the Panathenaic procession. Two wings projected forward; the north one held paintings, described by Pausanias. A planned south-eastern hall was never built, and some blocks still carry their unremoved lifting bosses, showing that the work stopped unfinished when war came in 431.

In later centuries the Propylaea became part of a palace of the Frankish dukes of Athens and then an Ottoman fortress. In 1656 lightning ignited gunpowder stored inside, causing a devastating explosion. Restoration has continued since the 19th century.

name: Temple of Athena Nike

claims.text: An Athenian decree commissioned the temple from the architect Callicrates; it was built in the 420s BC.
Its parapet was carved with Victories, including the famous 'Nike adjusting her sandal'.
The Ottomans dismantled the temple in 1686 to build a gun emplacement; it was reassembled in the 1830s.

milestones.text: Taken down by the Ottomans and built into a bastion before the Venetian siege
Reassembled from its recovered blocks by Ludwig Ross and colleagues

summary: The small Ionic temple of Athena as goddess of victory, built on a bastion at the entrance to the Acropolis in the 420s BC.
significance: A jewel of the Ionic order, whose sculptured parapet of Victories is among the most graceful works of classical art.
body:
The temple of Athena Nike stands on a high bastion to the right of the entrance to the Acropolis, where an older shrine of Athena as giver of victory had stood. An inscription, usually dated around 448 BC, ordered a temple to be built to the design of Callicrates, but construction took place only in the 420s, during the Peloponnesian War.

It is a small Ionic temple with four slender columns at front and back. Its frieze showed the gods and battles of Greeks against Persians and Greeks, a rare depiction of historical warfare on a temple. Around the edge of the bastion ran a marble parapet carved with winged Victories leading cattle to sacrifice and setting up trophies; the best known, "Nike adjusting her sandal", with drapery clinging like wet cloth, is in the Acropolis Museum.

In 1686, preparing for a Venetian attack, the Ottomans dismantled the temple and used its blocks in a gun emplacement. After Greek independence the blocks were recovered and the temple was reassembled in 1835–36. It has been dismantled and rebuilt twice since, most recently in a restoration completed in 2010, to correct earlier errors and repair damage.

name: Theatre of Dionysus

claims.text: The theatre stood on the south slope of the Acropolis within the sanctuary of Dionysus Eleuthereus.
The tragedies and comedies of Aeschylus, Sophocles, Euripides and Aristophanes were first staged at the City Dionysia in or beside this precinct.
The surviving stone auditorium belongs largely to a rebuilding of the later fourth century BC associated with the statesman Lycurgus.
The early theatre had a simple wooden or earthen arrangement, and its precise form in the fifth century BC is debated.

milestones.text: The theatre is rebuilt in stone under the statesman Lycurgus.
Excavation begins to uncover the theatre on the south slope of the Acropolis.

summary: The great open-air theatre on the south slope of the Acropolis, where the masterpieces of Athenian tragedy and comedy were first performed.
significance: The birthplace of European drama and the model for later Greek theatres.
body:
The Theatre of Dionysus lies on the south slope of the Acropolis, within the sanctuary of Dionysus Eleuthereus. It was the main venue of the City Dionysia, the spring festival at which the plays of Aeschylus, Sophocles, Euripides and Aristophanes were presented in competition before a mass audience.

In the fifth century BC the audience probably sat on timber seating or on the bare hillside, facing a circular dancing floor, the orchestra. The stone theatre seen today owes most to a rebuilding of the later fourth century BC, usually linked to the Athenian statesman Lycurgus, who also had standard texts of the three great tragedians deposited in the city's archive. The seating held on the order of fifteen thousand people.

The theatre was altered repeatedly in Hellenistic and Roman times, when the stage was rebuilt and marble thrones were installed for priests and officials; the central seat belonged to the priest of Dionysus Eleuthereus. Excavation began in the 1860s, and the site is now one of the best-known monuments of ancient Athens.

name: Hephaisteion

claims.text: The Hephaisteion is a Doric temple on Kolonos Agoraios, the hill overlooking the west side of the Athenian Agora.
Construction began around 449 BC and the building was probably completed in the 410s BC.
It was dedicated to Hephaestus and Athena, patrons of craftsmen, who worked in the workshops nearby.
It survived almost intact because it was converted into a Christian church, later called St George Akamates.

milestones.text: The last church services are held in the building before it becomes a museum.
The American School of Classical Studies begins digging the Agora below the temple.

summary: A Doric temple above the Athenian Agora, begun around 449 BC and the best-preserved ancient Greek temple in existence.
significance: The best-preserved Doric temple surviving from the ancient world, kept intact by centuries of use as a church.
body:
The Hephaisteion stands on Kolonos Agoraios, the low hill on the west side of the Agora of Athens. It was begun about 449 BC, in the years when Pericles' building programme was reshaping the city, and was completed in the following decades. The temple was dedicated to Hephaestus, god of the forge, and to Athena, and the surrounding district housed metalworkers and potters.

The building is a Doric peripteral temple of six by thirteen columns, in Pentelic marble with sculpted metopes and a frieze. Its design is close in spirit to the Parthenon, and the architect, who is unknown, appears to have worked on other temples in Attica.

It was long called the Theseion, from a mistaken belief that it housed the bones of Theseus. In the seventh century AD it was turned into the church of St George Akamates and remained in use until 1834. This continuous use explains its remarkable state of preservation. The American excavations of the Agora from 1931 cleared its surroundings and established its real dedication.

name: Kerameikos

claims.text: The Kerameikos was the potters' quarter of Athens and also its principal cemetery, lying outside the city wall on the northwest.
The Dipylon and Sacred Gates, the main gates of Athens, stood at the site and the Sacred Way to Eleusis began there.
Large Geometric grave vases such as the Dipylon amphorae were used as grave markers in the cemetery.
The annual funeral oration for the Athenian war dead was delivered here, according to Thucydides.

milestones.text: The German Archaeological Institute begins systematic excavation of the cemetery.

summary: The potters' quarter and chief cemetery of ancient Athens, lying northwest of the Agora beyond the city wall.
significance: The best source for Athenian burial customs, from Geometric vases to classical grave monuments.
body:
The Kerameikos takes its name from the Athenian potters (*kerameis*) who worked beside the Eridanos stream northwest of the Agora. It was also the city's main burial ground, used from the Bronze Age through to the Roman period, and the Dipylon and Sacred Gates of the city wall stood on the site. The Sacred Way, along which the Eleusinian procession passed, began here.

In the eighth century BC wealthy families marked graves with huge Geometric vases, the Dipylon amphorae, painted with funeral scenes. In the classical period grave monuments grew elaborate, with sculpted stelai and family plots lining the roads; later restrictions on display reduced their scale. Thucydides places the public burial of Athens' war dead nearby, where Pericles delivered the funeral speech he gives him.

The German Archaeological Institute has excavated the site since 1913, and the open-air museum there shows grave monuments in place. Finds from the area underpin much of the study of Athenian pottery and funerary art.

name: Pnyx

claims.text: The Pnyx was the hillside meeting place of the Athenian Assembly (Ekklesia) on a rise west of the Acropolis.
Excavation distinguishes three main building phases, the earliest probably around the end of the sixth century BC and the last in the later fourth century BC.
Speakers addressed the crowd from a stepped platform, the bema, cut into the rock.
The date of the first phase is debated, and some scholars place it later in the fifth century BC.

milestones.text: Excavations led by Kourouniotis and Thompson clarify the building phases of the Pnyx.

summary: The hill west of the Acropolis where the Athenian Assembly met to vote on war, peace, laws and ostracisms.
significance: The physical home of Athenian direct democracy, where citizens debated and decided state policy.
body:
The Pnyx is a rocky hill west of the Acropolis, whose slope was shaped into an assembly ground for the Athenian Ekklesia. Citizens sat on the ground or on benches and faced a stepped speakers' platform, the bema. The Assembly met around forty times a year to decide on war, treaties, finance and legislation, and any citizen could speak.

Excavations show three main phases. The earliest is generally linked with the democratic reforms of Cleisthenes, though some scholars place it later; the second dates around 400 BC; and the last, in the later fourth century BC, enlarged the space with a great retaining wall. The capacity of the assembly place was several thousand, but the quorum for some votes was 6,000, and the number of citizens actually present was often less.

In the late fourth century BC the Assembly began to meet more often in the Theatre of Dionysus. Speeches by Pericles, Cleon and Demosthenes are associated with the Pnyx in the literary record, and the site is now an open archaeological park.

name: Stoa of Attalos

claims.text: The stoa was a two-storey colonnaded market building on the east side of the Athenian Agora.
It was a gift to Athens from Attalus II, king of Pergamon, probably built between 159 and 138 BC.
It was burned in the Herulian sack of AD 267 and later incorporated into a late Roman fortification.
The stoa was rebuilt from 1953 to 1956 by the American School of Classical Studies with funding from John D. Rockefeller Jr.

milestones.text: The stoa is burned during the Herulian raid on Athens.
The reconstructed stoa opens as the museum of the Athenian Agora excavations.

summary: A two-storey colonnade on the east side of the Athenian Agora given to the city by Attalus II of Pergamon, and now rebuilt as the Agora museum.
significance: One of the few ancient Greek public buildings reconstructed on its original site, showing how a Hellenistic market building looked.
body:
The Stoa of Attalos was built in the mid-second century BC by Attalus II, king of Pergamon, who had studied in Athens and wished to show goodwill to the city. It formed the east boundary of the Agora: a long, two-storey colonnade of Doric columns outside and Ionic within, with twenty-one shops opening off each floor and a broad walkway in front.

Market stalls, offices and promenades filled such stoas, and this one became a busy commercial and social centre. It was burned in the Herulian raid of AD 267, and its ruins were built into the late Roman wall that crosses the Agora.

The American School of Classical Studies cleared the site in the 1930s and, funded by John D. Rockefeller Jr., rebuilt the stoa in 1953–56 from the surviving foundations and fragments. It houses the Museum of the Ancient Agora.

name: Tower of the Winds

claims.text: The Tower of the Winds is an octagonal marble building on the Roman Agora of Athens, designed as a combined water clock, sundial and weather vane.
Each side bears a relief of the wind that blows from that direction, and sundials are carved below them.
It was built by the astronomer Andronikos of Kyrrhos, according to the Roman author Varro, probably in the first century BC.
The building's exact date is debated, with proposals from the second century BC to the early first century BC.

summary: An octagonal marble clock tower in the Roman Agora of Athens, carved with the eight winds and equipped with sundials and a water clock.
significance: One of the earliest known meteorological stations and the best-preserved ancient timekeeping building.
body:
The Tower of the Winds is an eight-sided Pentelic marble tower about twelve metres high, standing on the Roman Agora east of the old Agora. Its builder, according to the Roman writer Varro, was Andronikos of Kyrrhos, and it is usually dated to the first century BC, though a second-century date has also been proposed.

Each face is decorated with a frieze figure for one of the eight winds, such as Boreas of the north and Zephyros of the west, and beneath each is a sundial. A bronze Triton, now lost, probably turned on the roof as a weather vane, and inside a water clock was fed from a cistern attached to the tower, giving time on cloudy days and at night.

The tower survived antiquity, was used by dervishes in Ottoman times, and was cleared of accumulated earth in the nineteenth century. A recent conservation programme reopened it to the public.

name: Mount Olympus

claims.text: At 2,917 metres Olympus is the highest mountain in Greece, on the border of Thessaly and Macedonia.
Homer places the home of the gods on Olympus, ruled by Zeus.
Later poets moved the gods' dwelling into the sky above the mountain, so that Olympus became a heavenly rather than a physical place.
The Macedonians held a festival to Zeus at Dion, at the foot of the mountain, and the sanctuary there was a major cult centre.
The first recorded modern ascent of the highest peak, Mytikas, was made in 1913.

milestones.text: Christos Kakalos with two Swiss climbers makes the first recorded ascent of Mytikas.

summary: The highest mountain in Greece, on the border of Macedonia and Thessaly, where the Greeks placed the home of Zeus and the Olympian gods.
significance: The mountain that gave its name to the Olympian gods and to the idea of a heavenly court of divine rulers.
body:
Mount Olympus rises in northern Greece, near the Thermaic Gulf, to 2,917 metres at the peak of Mytikas. Its summit is often hidden in cloud, and it was easily seen as a dwelling place for gods.

In Homer the gods feast in halls on Olympus, hold assemblies there and gaze down on the fighting at Troy. In Hesiod's *Theogony*, Zeus and his siblings fight the Titans from the mountain. Later authors, including Pindar and the tragedians, increasingly treat Olympus as an unreachable abode in the sky rather than an actual mountain, though cult at Dion on its slopes kept the physical mountain sacred.

In the Bronze Age the area was an important route between Macedonia and Thessaly. The summit was first climbed in 1913, and the mountain, now a national park and UNESCO biosphere reserve, remains an emblem of Greek mythology.

name: Mount Parnassus

claims.text: Parnassus rises to about 2,457 metres above Delphi, which lies on its southern slope.
The mountain was sacred to Apollo, to Dionysus and to the Muses.
The Corycian Cave on the mountain was a cult place of Pan and the nymphs, and offerings have been found there.
In myth the flood hero Deucalion landed on Parnassus after the great flood.

summary: The limestone massif above Delphi in Phocis, sacred to Apollo, the Muses and Dionysus and a symbol of poetry in later Europe.
significance: The mountain of Apollo and the Muses, whose name became shorthand for poetry and learning.
body:
Parnassus is a high limestone massif in central Greece, reaching about 2,457 metres. Delphi stands on its southern foot, below the cliffs of the Phaedriades, and the Castalian spring, where pilgrims purified themselves, emerges from a cleft in the rock.

The mountain was shared between gods. Apollo and the Muses were associated with its upper slopes and with poetic inspiration; in winter, Dionysus was honoured there by women known as Thyiades who climbed to the mountain for night-time rites. The Corycian Cave, high above Delphi, was sacred to Pan and the nymphs, and excavations there have recovered large numbers of knucklebones, lamps and other offerings.

In myth Deucalion's ark came to rest on Parnassus after the flood. In later Europe the name became a metaphor for the world of poets: the Parnassian poets of nineteenth-century France took their name from it.

name: Temple of Apollo at Delphi

claims.text: The temple housed the Pythia, Apollo's priestess, who gave oracles in an inner chamber called the adyton.
An earlier temple was destroyed by fire in 548 BC and rebuilt in the late sixth century BC, a project Herodotus says the Athenian Alcmaeonid family helped finance.
That temple was wrecked in 373 BC by an earthquake and replaced by the Doric temple whose foundations survive, built between about 366 and 329 BC.
The maxims 'Know thyself' and 'Nothing in excess' were inscribed in the forecourt according to Pausanias.

milestones.text: The French School at Athens begins to uncover the temple terrace.
Six columns of the temple are re-erected at the site.

summary: The Doric temple of Apollo at Delphi, in whose inner chamber the Pythia delivered the oracle consulted across the Greek world.
significance: The heart of the most important oracle in the ancient world.
body:
The temple of Apollo stood on a terrace above the Sacred Way at Delphi. Tradition recalled several earlier temples, and a stone building of the sixth century BC burned in 548 BC. Herodotus says it was rebuilt with funds from across Greece and that the Alcmaeonid family of Athens, then in exile, paid for a marble front. In 373 BC the temple was wrecked, probably by an earthquake.

The temple whose foundations are visible today was built between about 366 and 329 BC. It was a Doric peripteral building of six by fifteen columns, with sculpture on its pediments. In the pronaos were inscribed Delphic maxims such as 'Know thyself', recorded by Pausanias. Inside, the *adyton* was a lower chamber in which the Pythia sat on a tripod, and where the omphalos and a flame burned continually.

Plutarch served as a priest here around AD 100. Pagan cult ended in the later fourth century AD. The French School at Athens excavated the site from 1892, and the six columns standing today were set up in 1938 from fallen pieces.

name: Temple of Hera at Olympia

claims.text: The Heraion at Olympia was built around 600 BC and is one of the earliest large Doric temples in Greece.
Its columns were replaced one by one in stone over the centuries, so that the colonnade shows a range of styles.
Pausanias saw the Hermes of Praxiteles inside the temple, and the statue was found in its remains in 1877.
Today the flame for the modern Olympic Games is lit before the temple by focusing sunlight with a mirror.

milestones.text: The Hermes of Praxiteles is found in the ruins of the temple by German excavators.
The modern Olympic flame is lit at the temple for the first time ahead of the Berlin Games.

summary: A Doric temple of about 600 BC at Olympia, dedicated to Hera, older than the great temple of Zeus and one of the oldest large stone temples in Greece.
significance: A key monument in the early history of Doric architecture, and the place where the modern Olympic flame is lit.
body:
The temple of Hera at Olympia was built around 600 BC and is one of the earliest large Doric temples in Greece. It is a long building of six by sixteen columns. Pausanias reports that one of the columns in its rear porch was still made of oak when he visited, which suggests that stone columns replaced wooden ones one at a time, and the surviving shafts do vary in proportion.

The temple held a gold and ivory image of Zeus and Hera and, in Pausanias' day, the Hermes of Praxiteles. Beside it stood the circular Philippeion and the altar on which the Olympic flame was kept. Women also ran a footrace here, the Heraia, in honour of Hera.

German excavations at Olympia from 1875 uncovered the temple, and the Hermes was found in its ruins in 1877. Since 1936 the temple has been the setting of the ceremony in which the torch for each modern Games is lit.

name: Smyrna

claims.text: Old Smyrna, at modern Bayraklı, was settled by Aeolian Greeks and became an Ionian city in the early first millennium BC.
The Lydian king Alyattes sacked the city around 600 BC, after which it survived only as scattered villages.
A new Smyrna was founded on Mount Pagos in the early Hellenistic period, associated with Antigonus and Lysimachus.
Smyrna was one of several cities that claimed to be the birthplace of Homer.
It became a leading city of Roman Asia and the home of Aelius Aristides.

milestones.text: Excavations at Bayraklı begin and reveal the walls and temple of Old Smyrna.

summary: A Greek city on the Aegean coast of Asia Minor, claimed by tradition as Homer's birthplace, destroyed about 600 BC and refounded in the Hellenistic period.
significance: A long-lived Ionian city, later the site of modern Izmir.
body:
Smyrna lay at the head of a deep gulf on the Aegean coast of what is now Turkey. The earliest Greek city, now called Old Smyrna, stood at Bayraklı on a peninsula. Aeolian Greeks settled there and it later joined the Ionian group of cities. Excavations show fortification walls from the ninth century BC onward and an early temple of Athena.

The city was one of those that claimed Homer, and it kept a shrine in his honour. Around 600 BC the Lydian king Alyattes captured the town, and it was left as villages for some three centuries. Smyrna was refounded on the slopes of Mount Pagos, probably under Antigonus and then Lysimachus, with a regular street plan.

Under Rome it was one of the great cities of Asia and a centre of the Second Sophistic. The orator Aelius Aristides lived near it and wrote about its rebuilding after the earthquake of about AD 178. It continued under Byzantine and later rulers as the city of Izmir.

name: Akragas

claims.text: Akragas was founded around 580 BC by colonists from Gela and Rhodes on the south coast of Sicily.
The tyrant Phalaris ruled in the sixth century BC and was said to have roasted victims in a bronze bull.
Under Theron, Akragas shared in the victory over Carthage at Himera in 480 BC and built the great temples of the Valley of the Temples.
The city was sacked by Carthage in 406 BC.
The philosopher Empedocles was born in Akragas.

milestones.text: The Valley of the Temples is inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List.

summary: A wealthy Greek colony on the south coast of Sicily, famous for the Doric temples of its Valley of the Temples and as the birthplace of Empedocles.
significance: One of the richest western Greek cities, with the best-preserved group of Greek temples outside Greece itself.
body:
Akragas was founded around 580 BC by Gelan and Rhodian colonists on a ridge overlooking the south coast of Sicily. Its early history is dominated by the tyrant Phalaris, remembered for cruelty, and by Theron, who ruled in the early fifth century BC. With Gelon of Syracuse, Theron defeated the Carthaginians at Himera in 480 BC, and prisoners and spoils from the war paid for monumental building.

The temples along the southern ridge, among them the so-called Temple of Concordia, one of the best-preserved Doric temples anywhere, and the huge Temple of Olympian Zeus, reflect the city's wealth. Diodorus describes Akragas as one of the most luxurious cities of the Greek world, and claims its population was very large, though his numbers are probably inflated.

Carthage sacked Akragas in 406 BC after a long siege, and it never fully recovered. It later came under Roman rule as Agrigentum. The site is now a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

name: Taras

claims.text: Taras was founded around 706 BC by Spartan colonists, according to tradition led by Phalanthus.
The city lay on a natural harbour in the heel of Italy and was the largest Greek city in Apulia.
The philosopher and statesman Archytas led Taras in the fourth century BC.
Taras called in Pyrrhus of Epirus against Rome, and fell to the Romans in 272 BC.

summary: A Spartan colony on the Gulf of Taranto in southern Italy, the leading Greek city of Apulia and ally of Pyrrhus against Rome.
significance: The one Spartan colony of note, and a rich city in the western Greek world.
body:
Taras, now Taranto, was founded about 706 BC by Spartans, according to tradition by the *Partheniai*, sons of Spartan women born during the long Messenian war. It lay on a peninsula enclosing a large natural harbour, and grew rich on fishing, dyeing with murex purple, and pottery and coinage.

In the fourth century BC the city was ruled by Archytas, a Pythagorean mathematician who was general of Taras several times. After his time Taras repeatedly called on foreign condottieri against local tribes, including Archidamus III of Sparta and Alexander of Epirus. In 282 BC the Tarentines attacked Roman ships and appealed to Pyrrhus, who came to Italy in 280.

After Pyrrhus withdrew, Taras was captured by Rome in 272 BC. It became a Roman ally, sided with Hannibal in 212 BC, and was sacked after the Romans retook it in 209.

name: Sybaris

claims.text: Sybaris was founded about 720 BC by Achaean colonists on the Gulf of Taranto.
Its wealth made 'sybarite' a byword for luxury.
The neighbouring city of Croton destroyed Sybaris in 510 BC.
The ruins lie deep under river silt and a rising water table, so the archaic city has been hard to excavate.

milestones.text: Excavations in the plain of Sibari begin to locate the successive cities.

summary: A rich Achaean colony in southern Italy, destroyed by its neighbour Croton in 510 BC and proverbial for luxury.
significance: Its name gave the language the word 'sybarite', and its fall is one of the best-known episodes of western Greek history.
body:
Sybaris was founded about 720 BC by Achaean settlers on the Gulf of Taranto, between two rivers. Its farmland was rich and it traded across southern Italy, sending goods overland to the Tyrrhenian coast where it had a daughter colony at Laos and a trading partner in the Etruscans.

Greek writers made the city a standard example of luxury, with stories about citizens who forbade noisy trades within the city and who trained horses to dance. Most of these tales are probably later moralising, but the city's wealth was real.

In 510 BC a conflict with neighbouring Croton ended with the city's destruction, according to tradition after Sybaris expelled the nobles who fled to Croton. The site was resettled several times, notably as the Athenian-sponsored colony of Thurii in 444/443 BC, but archaic Sybaris lies deep below silt, which has made it hard to study.

name: Cumae

claims.text: Cumae was founded around the 740s–720s BC by Euboean settlers from Chalcis and Eretria, and is regarded as the earliest Greek colony on the Italian mainland.
The Greek alphabet used at Cumae was passed to the Etruscans and from them to Rome.
Hieron I of Syracuse defeated an Etruscan fleet off Cumae in 474 BC.
A cave beneath the acropolis was identified in Antiquity as the seat of the Sibyl of Cumae.

milestones.text: Excavations by Amedeo Maiuri uncover the acropolis temples and the so-called Sibyl's cave.

summary: The first Greek colony on the Italian mainland, founded by Euboeans on the coast of Campania, and the place through which the Greek alphabet reached Rome.
significance: An early gateway between the Greek and Italian worlds.
body:
Cumae was founded by settlers from Chalcis and Eretria, probably in the mid-eighth century BC, a little after their trading post on the island of Pithekoussai (Ischia). It stood on a coastal hill north of the Bay of Naples and ruled a fertile plain, and for a time was the most powerful Greek city in the region.

Through contact with Etruscans and Latins, Cumae seems to have passed on the Euboean form of the Greek alphabet, from which the Etruscan and then the Latin alphabets derive. In 474 BC the Cumaeans appealed to Hieron I of Syracuse, whose fleet destroyed an Etruscan force off the coast and weakened Etruscan power in the south.

In 421 BC the city fell to the Samnites. Later it was a Roman town. In Roman tradition it was the home of the Sibyl who guided Aeneas, and a vaulted gallery on the acropolis has long been shown as her cave, although archaeologists doubt the link.

name: Selinus

claims.text: Selinus was founded around 628 BC by colonists from Megara Hyblaea on the south-west coast of Sicily.
The city's several large Doric temples, now designated by letters, include some of the largest in the Greek world.
A border dispute with Segesta led Segesta to appeal to Athens, which sent the Sicilian expedition in 415 BC.
Carthage destroyed the city in 409 BC.

milestones.text: British excavators uncover sculptured metopes from the temples of the acropolis.

summary: A Greek colony in south-west Sicily, notable for its monumental temples and for its quarrel with Segesta, which drew Athens into Sicily.
significance: One of the best-preserved temple complexes of the western Greeks, and a cause of the Athenian Sicilian expedition.
body:
Selinus was founded about 628 BC by Megarian colonists from Megara Hyblaea on the south-west coast of Sicily, at the frontier with Carthaginian and Elymian territory. It prospered from farmland and trade, and its wealth is visible in temples on the acropolis and on the eastern hill.

These are the largest Doric temples of the western Greeks. Temple G, never finished, was among the biggest of the Greek world, and sculpted metopes from earlier temples, now in the museum at Palermo, show the archaic Sicilian style. Selinus also produced a famous series of silver coins showing a celery leaf, the plant for which the city was named.

War with Segesta over borderland led Segesta to ask Athens for help in 416 BC. The Athenians sent an expedition that ended in disaster. In 409 BC a Carthaginian army took Selinus by storm and slaughtered much of its population. The city was partly resettled under Carthaginian control and finally abandoned in the third century BC.

name: Segesta

claims.text: Segesta was a city of the Elymians, one of the native peoples of western Sicily, that adopted Greek culture.
Its Doric temple, begun around 430–420 BC, was never finished: the columns are unfluted and the cella was never built.
The city's request for Athenian aid against Selinus in 416 BC led to the Sicilian expedition.
The Segestans were said to have tricked the Athenian envoys by borrowing treasure to display, according to Thucydides.

summary: A native Elymian city of western Sicily, deeply influenced by Greek culture, whose appeal to Athens in 416 BC helped bring about the Sicilian expedition.
significance: Its unfinished Doric temple is one of the most striking classical ruins in Sicily, and its feud with Selinus helped set off a major war.
body:
Segesta, in the hills of north-west Sicily, belonged to the Elymians, a people the Greeks believed descended from Trojan refugees. By the fifth century BC the city used Greek architecture, coinage and, in part, the Greek language, though its alliances were often with Carthage.

Its best-known monument, a large Doric temple on a hill outside the town, was begun about 430–420 BC and left unfinished, perhaps because of the war with Selinus. Its columns still lack fluting. A theatre on the summit of the city hill, built in the Hellenistic period, looks over the Gulf of Castellammare.

Segesta fought a border war with Selinus, and in 416 BC asked Athens for aid. According to Thucydides, the Segestans promised money they did not have and deceived Athenian envoys with borrowed plate; Athens sent the great expedition of 415 BC. The city later passed between Carthaginian, Syracusan and Roman control.

name: Priene

claims.text: Priene was an Ionian city at the mouth of the Meander that moved to its present site about the mid-fourth century BC after silting of the old harbour.
The new city was laid out on a regular grid of streets on terraces below a steep rock.
The temple of Athena Polias was designed by the architect Pytheos, who also worked on the Mausoleum at Halicarnassus.
An inscription records that Alexander the Great dedicated the temple.

milestones.text: Excavations by Carl Humann and Theodor Wiegand begin to uncover the Hellenistic town.

summary: A small Ionian city rebuilt in the fourth century BC on a regular grid below a steep rock, and the best-preserved example of a planned Hellenistic town.
significance: A well-preserved Greek town showing how a planned city worked, with houses, assembly hall, theatre and gymnasium all surviving.
body:
Priene was an Ionian city of the Panionian league. Its harbour on the Meander silted up, and in the mid-fourth century BC the city moved a few kilometres to a steep terraced site. The new town was laid out on a grid, with streets running east–west and north–south, and its public buildings, among them the agora, the council house, the theatre and the gymnasium, are unusually well preserved.

The temple of Athena Polias was designed by Pytheos, who wrote a book about it and also worked on the Mausoleum. An inscription found on the temple records Alexander's dedication in 334 BC, when he passed through Ionia. Houses of the period, mostly of a standard plan around a courtyard, survive in numbers, and show the standard of living of Hellenistic citizens.

The river continued to silt up, and Priene gradually declined, though it survived under Roman and Byzantine rule. German excavators started work in 1895.

name: Didyma

claims.text: Didyma was an oracular sanctuary of Apollo about 20 km south of Miletus, connected to the city by a Sacred Way.
The archaic temple was destroyed by the Persians after the Ionian Revolt, probably in 494 BC.
A giant new temple, begun around 300 BC by the architects Paionios of Ephesus and Daphnis of Miletus, was never finished.
Seleucus I returned the cult statue of Apollo that Xerxes was said to have carried off.

milestones.text: German excavators led by Theodor Wiegand begin work on the great temple.

summary: The oracular sanctuary of Apollo near Miletus, whose colossal Hellenistic temple was never completed.
significance: The most important oracle in Asia Minor, and one of the largest Greek temples ever begun.
body:
Didyma lay on the coast of Ionia about 20 kilometres south of Miletus, to which it was joined by a Sacred Way lined with statues. It housed an oracle of Apollo run by the Branchidae, a priestly family, and was consulted by cities and kings. Herodotus reports that Croesus sent gifts to it.

The archaic temple was destroyed after the Ionian Revolt. Tradition says the Persians removed Apollo's bronze statue, and that Seleucus I restored it in the early third century BC. About 300 BC the Milesians began a vast new temple, designed by Paionios of Ephesus and Daphnis of Miletus. It was a double-colonnaded building with an unroofed inner court enclosing a small shrine, and was still unfinished centuries later.

The oracle faded after Christianity became the official religion, and a church was built inside the ruins. German archaeologists have excavated the site since 1905.

name: Amphipolis

claims.text: Athens founded Amphipolis in 437/436 BC under Hagnon on the river Strymon, in a region rich in timber and silver.
The Spartan general Brasidas captured the city in 424 BC, and the historian Thucydides, who commanded the Athenian fleet nearby, was exiled for failing to prevent it.
Philip II of Macedon took Amphipolis in 357 BC, which started a long war with Athens.
A large burial mound of the late fourth century BC, the Kasta Tomb, was excavated in 2012–14.

milestones.text: The Lion of Amphipolis, a large funerary monument, is found in the Strymon's river bed.
Excavation of the Kasta Tomb reveals its caryatids and mosaic floor.

summary: An Athenian colony on the river Strymon in Macedonia, whose capture by Brasidas in 424 BC and by Philip II in 357 BC both changed the course of Greek history.
significance: A city whose loss cost Athens its northern timber and silver and led to the exile of Thucydides.
body:
Amphipolis was founded by Athens in 437/436 BC at a bend of the Strymon, in a region that supplied timber for ships and silver from the Pangaion mines. The Athenian general Hagnon led the settlers, who were joined by local Thracians.

In the winter of 424 BC the Spartan Brasidas approached the city suddenly and offered generous terms. Thucydides, commanding Athenian ships at Thasos, arrived too late to save it and was sent into exile, which gave him the time to write his history. In 422 BC Cleon and Brasidas both died fighting outside its walls. The Peace of Nicias required Sparta to return the city, but Amphipolis never rejoined Athens.

Philip II captured the city in 357 BC, gaining control of the mines, and it remained Macedonian. Excavations since 2012 have focused on the Kasta Tomb, a huge mound whose burial chamber has caryatids and a mosaic.

name: Potidaea

claims.text: Potidaea was founded by Corinth around 600 BC on the isthmus of the Pallene peninsula.
Its revolt from the Athenian Empire in 432 BC and Athens' siege of the city was one of the immediate causes of the Peloponnesian War.
Socrates served at the siege as a hoplite and saved the life of Alcibiades, according to Plato.
The city fell to Athens in 430/429 BC after a siege during which the garrison ate human flesh, according to Thucydides.
Philip II took Potidaea in 356 BC, and Cassander refounded the city in 316 BC as Cassandreia.

summary: A Corinthian colony on the Pallene peninsula whose revolt from Athens in 432 BC and long siege helped bring on the Peloponnesian War.
significance: A flashpoint between Athens and Corinth in the years before the Peloponnesian War, and the setting for Socrates' military service.
body:
Potidaea stood on the narrowest part of the Pallene peninsula in Chalcidice, in northern Greece. It was founded by Corinth around 600 BC but later paid tribute to the Athenian Empire. In 433/432 BC, Athens demanded that it tear down its walls on the seaward side, dismiss its Corinthian magistrates and give hostages. Potidaea revolted with Corinthian help, and Athens laid siege.

The Corinthians appealed to Sparta, and Thucydides counts the affair among the immediate causes of the war. The siege lasted until 430/429 BC, at a cost of two thousand talents; the city surrendered on terms and its people were expelled. Plato's Socrates says he served in the siege and fought bravely, and that he saved Alcibiades after he was wounded.

Athens settled its own colonists there, but the city was taken by Philip II in 356 BC. In 316 BC Cassander refounded it under his own name as Cassandreia, which became an important Macedonian city.

name: Chalcis

claims.text: Chalcis was a leading Euboean city that controlled the narrow strait of the Euripus.
Chalcis sent colonists to Chalcidice, southern Italy and Sicily, including Cumae, Rhegion and Naxos in Sicily.
It fought the Lelantine War against neighbouring Eretria, apparently over the Lelantine plain.
Athens defeated Chalcis in 506 BC and settled four thousand cleruchs on its land.

summary: The leading city of Euboea in the eighth and seventh centuries BC, a major colonising power and rival of Eretria.
significance: One of the most active city-founders of the colonising age, which passed the Euboean alphabet and trade west.
body:
Chalcis lay on the narrowest point of the Euripus, the channel between Euboea and the mainland. Its name may mean the 'bronze' city, and it was rich in metals and trade. In the eighth century BC it was a major sender of colonists, who founded cities in Chalcidice, which takes its name from them, and in the west, with Cumae in Campania, Naxos and Zancle in Sicily and Rhegion in Italy.

The city's long rivalry with Eretria is remembered as the Lelantine War, the first conflict said to have drawn in other Greek states. Archaeologists connect the decline of Lefkandi around 700 BC with this period, though details of the war remain uncertain.

In 506 BC the young Athenian democracy defeated Chalcis and shared out its best land among Athenian settlers. It stayed under Athens until 446 BC, and after that formed part of the Euboean league. The modern city of Chalkida continues on the site.

name: Messene

claims.text: Messene was founded in 369 BC, with the support of Thebes and Epaminondas, to give the Messenians a capital after Sparta's defeat at Leuctra.
The city stood under Mount Ithome, the old Messenian stronghold, and was enclosed by a nine-kilometre circuit of fine ashlar walls.
Its Asclepieion, theatre, council house and stadium were built in the Hellenistic period.
Systematic excavation has continued since 1986 under Petros Themelis.

milestones.text: Systematic excavation of the city begins under Petros Themelis.

summary: The capital founded in 369 BC for the freed Messenians, protected by one of the finest circuits of fortifications in the Greek world.
significance: A symbol of the end of Spartan hegemony, and now one of the best-preserved Hellenistic cities in Greece.
body:
After the Theban victory at Leuctra in 371 BC, Epaminondas marched into the Peloponnese and invaded Laconia. In 369 BC he helped the Messenians, who had been held as helots by Sparta for generations, to found a city of their own at the foot of Mount Ithome. Its construction was celebrated with sacrifices and flute music, and it deprived Sparta of the land and labour on which its society depended.

The city walls ran for nine kilometres and had towers and gates, among them the Arcadian Gate, which still stands. Pausanias describes a city with a great marketplace, a sanctuary of Asclepius, a theatre and a stadium surrounded by statues, much of which excavation has since confirmed.

Messene was independent until the Achaean League took it in the second century BC, and flourished under Roman rule. Excavations since 1986 have uncovered the Asclepieion and a stadium with a colonnade that is among the best preserved in Greece.

name: Megalopolis

claims.text: Megalopolis was founded around 371–368 BC as the capital of the Arcadian League with Theban encouragement, to counter Sparta.
It was built by gathering the people of many villages into one city on the river Helisson.
The city's theatre, with a capacity of around 20,000, was possibly the largest in Greece, and beside it stood the Thersilion, a hall for the League assembly.
Sparta under Cleomenes III sacked the city in 223 BC, and its citizens included the statesman Philopoemen and the historian Polybius.

milestones.text: The British School at Athens excavates the theatre and the Thersilion.

summary: A planned city founded in the 360s BC as the capital of the Arcadian League, home to the largest theatre in Greece and to the historian Polybius.
significance: A deliberate act of city-building meant to block Spartan power in the Peloponnese, and the home city of Polybius.
body:
Megalopolis, 'the great city', was founded in about 371–368 BC after the Theban victory at Leuctra weakened Sparta. Arcadian villages were joined in a single city beside the Helisson to provide an Arcadian League with a capital and to guard the north of Laconia against Spartan revenge. Epaminondas encouraged the project.

The city's theatre was among the largest in Greece, and beside it stood the Thersilion, a roofed assembly hall with the seats radiating from the centre, built to hold the Ten Thousand delegates of the League. The British School at Athens excavated both in the 1890s.

Megalopolis stood by Macedon against Sparta, and joined the Achaean League in 235 BC. In 223 BC Cleomenes III took and destroyed much of the city. Philopoemen, the last great Achaean general, and Polybius, who wrote the history of Rome's rise, were both from Megalopolis. The city declined after the Roman conquest, and Pausanias found it largely deserted.

name: Tegea

claims.text: Tegea was the leading city of eastern Arcadia, with a sanctuary of Athena Alea.
After long wars, Sparta made Tegea an ally in about 550 BC, according to Herodotus, partly after finding bones said to be those of Orestes.
The temple of Athena Alea was rebuilt in the fourth century BC, with sculpture by Scopas.
Tegea sent a contingent to Plataea in 479 BC.

milestones.text: The French School at Athens first excavates the temple of Athena Alea.

summary: The chief city of eastern Arcadia and a long-time Spartan ally, famous for its temple of Athena Alea designed by Scopas.
significance: A major sanctuary and an example of how Sparta turned former rivals into allies.
body:
Tegea lay on the plain of Arcadia on the route between Sparta and Argos. For long it was Sparta's chief rival in the northern Peloponnese, and Herodotus describes battles in which the Spartans were beaten and Spartan prisoners were set to work in the Tegean fields in chains. Around 550 BC Sparta, advised by Delphi, recovered what it believed were the bones of Orestes from Tegean ground, and Tegea afterwards became a loyal ally.

The Tegean contingent fought at Plataea. After Leuctra, Tegea joined the Arcadian League and was one of the cities that sided against Sparta, but its position near the Laconian border kept its fortunes tied to Spartan power.

The temple of Athena Alea was rebuilt in the fourth century BC by the sculptor Scopas of Paros, after a fire of 395 BC. Pausanias admired its size and decoration, which included the tusks of the Calydonian boar. French excavations in the late nineteenth century and Norwegian ones in the 1990s have recovered its plan.

name: Susa

claims.text: Susa was an ancient Elamite city that Darius I made an administrative capital of the Persian Empire.
The Royal Road ran from Susa to Sardis, a journey of about 2,500 km.
Darius' foundation inscription describes materials and craftsmen brought from across the empire to build his palace at Susa.
Alexander took Susa in 331 BC without a fight and held a mass wedding there in 324 BC.

milestones.text: Marcel Dieulafoy's French expedition begins to uncover the Achaemenid palace of Darius.

summary: An ancient city of south-western Iran that Darius I made an administrative capital of the Persian Empire, and where Alexander held his mass wedding in 324 BC.
significance: A principal capital of the empire the Greeks fought in the Persian Wars and Alexander conquered.
body:
Susa lay in the lowlands of Elam, in south-west Iran. It was already about three thousand years old when Cyrus the Great's empire absorbed it. Darius I rebuilt it from around 520 BC as a main royal residence, and it served as the winter capital of the Achaemenid court. He built a palace with a great audience hall and enamelled brick friezes, and his foundation inscriptions list materials from Lebanon, Ionia, India and Egypt.

The Royal Road, a staffed highway of the Persian state with relay stations, connected Susa to Sardis. Greek writers knew the city as the seat of the king: Aeschylus' *Persians* is set there. After Gaugamela, Alexander captured Susa with its treasury, and in 324 BC he married the daughter of Darius III there while about eighty of his companions married Persian noblewomen.

French excavators, starting with Marcel Dieulafoy in the 1880s, uncovered the palace and recovered glazed-brick friezes, now in the Louvre.

name: Gordion

claims.text: Gordion was the capital of the Phrygian kingdom, on the Sakarya river in central Anatolia.
The largest burial mound, Tumulus MM, held a wooden tomb chamber of about 740 BC, the oldest standing wooden building known, and a rich assemblage of bronze vessels.
Greek tradition said the Phrygian king Midas and his father Gordias ruled from Gordion.
Alexander the Great visited Gordion in 333 BC and cut or loosened the Gordian knot, which was said to promise rule over Asia.
The occupant of Tumulus MM is traditionally identified as a Phrygian king, often assumed to be Midas' father, though the identification is uncertain.

milestones.text: The University of Pennsylvania begins excavating Gordion under Rodney Young.
Tumulus MM is opened and its wooden tomb chamber is found intact.

summary: The Phrygian capital in central Anatolia, home of the legendary King Midas and the site of Alexander's encounter with the Gordian knot.
significance: The best-excavated Phrygian site, whose great tumulus tombs show the wealth of a kingdom known to Greeks mainly through myth.
body:
Gordion stood on the Sakarya river in the Anatolian plateau, about 100 kilometres from modern Ankara. It was the capital of the Phrygians, whose kings, in Greek tradition named Gordias and Midas, ruled central Anatolia in the eighth and seventh centuries BC. A fortified citadel with monumental gateways, a series of large halls and workshops, and a cluster of burial mounds have been excavated.

The largest mound, Tumulus MM, covers a log chamber built about 740 BC in which a man was buried with a huge collection of bronze bowls, jugs and inlaid wooden tables. The site was damaged by fire in the early period and later rebuilt, and became part of the Lydian kingdom and then of the Persian Empire.

In 333 BC Alexander came to Gordion and was shown the wagon of Gordias, whose yoke was tied with a knot that, according to tradition, would give its undoer control of Asia. Accounts differ on whether he sliced through it with his sword or removed the pin. The University of Pennsylvania has excavated the site since 1950.

name: Stagira

claims.text: Stagira was founded about 655 BC by colonists from Andros on the coast of Chalcidice.
Aristotle was born in Stagira in 384 BC, the son of a doctor at the Macedonian court.
Philip II destroyed the city in 349 BC during his conquest of Chalcidice.
Tradition says Philip later rebuilt the city and resettled its people at Aristotle's request.

milestones.text: Greek archaeologists begin sustained excavation of the walls and acropolis of Stagira.

summary: A small colony in Chalcidice, remembered as the birthplace of Aristotle and destroyed by Philip II in 349 BC.
significance: The home town of Aristotle, whose philosophy shaped western thought.
body:
Stagira was a small harbour town on the eastern coast of Chalcidice, in northern Greece, founded about 655 BC by settlers from Andros. It was tributary to Athens in the fifth century BC and later joined the Chalcidian league.

Aristotle was born there in 384 BC. His father Nicomachus was physician to the Macedonian king Amyntas III, and the philosopher's ties to the Macedonian court shaped his career, as he later became tutor of the young Alexander. Philip II captured and destroyed Stagira during his campaign against the Chalcidian cities in 349 BC. A later tradition, recorded by Plutarch and others, says Philip restored the city and its exiles as a favour to Aristotle, although how far this is true is uncertain.

The site, on a peninsula near modern Olympiada, has been excavated since the 1990s. It shows fortification walls, houses and a sanctuary.

name: Chios

claims.text: Chios was one of the twelve Ionian cities, an island off the coast of Asia Minor.
The island was a producer of wine and mastic, and a centre of the Greek slave trade.
The Homeridae, a guild of rhapsodes, were said to live on Chios and claim descent from Homer.
Chios stayed loyal to Athens until its revolt in 412 BC, near the end of the Peloponnesian War.
In 1822, Ottoman troops massacred a large part of the island's population during the Greek War of Independence.

milestones.text: Ottoman forces massacre and enslave much of the island's population.

summary: A large Ionian island off the coast of Asia Minor, famous for wine, mastic, a guild claiming descent from Homer, and the 1822 massacre.
significance: A leading Aegean state which remained loyal to Athens until 412 BC, and which suffered one of the worst atrocities of the Greek War of Independence.
body:
Chios lies in the eastern Aegean, a few kilometres from the coast of Asia Minor. It was among the twelve Ionian cities, and an early centre of commerce, producing wine that was widely exported and the aromatic resin called mastic. Chios was also noted for its ships and for being one of the first Greek states to buy slaves from non-Greek lands.

The island was home to the Homeridae, whose members claimed descent from Homer and recited his poems. The poet and tragedian Ion and the historian Theopompus were born there. Chios supplied ships to Athens as an autonomous member of the Delian League, and in 412 BC rebelled against it with Spartan help during the Peloponnesian War. The island kept an independent identity under Roman and Byzantine rule, and under the Genoese from 1346 to 1566.

In April 1822 Ottoman forces landed after a local rising and killed or enslaved tens of thousands of inhabitants. The event moved western opinion and inspired a painting by Delacroix.

name: Kos

claims.text: Hippocrates was born on Kos around 460 BC and the island became a centre of medical teaching.
The Asclepieion of Kos was a healing sanctuary built on terraces above the city in the Hellenistic period.
Ptolemy II Philadelphus was born on Kos in 309 BC.
The poets Philitas and Theocritus were associated with Kos in the early Hellenistic period.

milestones.text: Rudolf Herzog uncovers the terraces of the Asclepieion.

summary: A Dodecanese island, birthplace of Hippocrates and Ptolemy II, with one of the most famous healing sanctuaries of antiquity.
significance: The island most associated with the beginnings of rational medicine.
body:
Kos is an island in the south-eastern Aegean, close to the Anatolian coast. Settled by Dorian Greeks, it was an early member of the Dorian Hexapolis. The physician Hippocrates was born there about 460 BC, and the medical school of Kos, which stressed careful observation and the natural causes of disease, was associated with him. A plane tree in the town is shown to visitors as the tree under which he taught, though it is much younger than that.

The Asclepieion of Kos, on terraces above the city, was built in the third century BC and continued to expand in later centuries. It combined a temple of Asclepius with baths, a gymnasium and a medical school, and drew pilgrims who sought cures.

Ptolemy II was born on Kos in 309 BC, and the island kept close ties with the Ptolemies. Excavations by Rudolf Herzog from 1902 revealed the sanctuary.

name: Naxos

claims.text: Naxos is the largest island of the Cyclades, noted for fine marble and emery.
Naxians dedicated the Lion Terrace and a colossal statue at Delos in the seventh century BC.
The unfinished doorway of a temple of Apollo, the Portara, dates to about 530 BC under the tyrant Lygdamis.
Myth says Theseus abandoned Ariadne on Naxos and Dionysus found her there.
A failed Persian-backed expedition against Naxos in 499 BC helped to start the Ionian Revolt.

summary: The largest of the Cyclades, famous for marble, early monumental sculpture and as the island where Dionysus found Ariadne.
significance: A leading sculptural centre of the archaic Aegean whose siege in 499 BC set off the Ionian Revolt.
body:
Naxos is the largest and most fertile of the Cyclades, with high mountains and quarries of fine marble and emery. It was inhabited from the Neolithic period and was a major centre of the early Cycladic culture, many of whose marble figurines come from its cemeteries.

In the seventh and sixth centuries BC, Naxos became one of the leading centres of marble sculpture in Greece. Its craftsmen exported large kouroi, and the Naxians dedicated a colossal statue and the row of marble lions at Delos. Quarries on the island still contain unfinished giant statues, one of them at Apollonas. The Portara, the giant marble doorway of an unfinished temple of Apollo, was begun about 530 BC under the tyrant Lygdamis and still stands by the harbour.

In myth, Theseus abandoned Ariadne on Naxos, where Dionysus found her. In 499 BC, Aristagoras of Miletus led a Persian-backed attack on Naxos that failed, an event Herodotus gives as the first cause of the Ionian Revolt.

name: Paros

claims.text: Paros produced the highly prized Parian marble, quarried underground at Marathi.
The poet Archilochus was born on Paros around 680 BC.
Miltiades led an unsuccessful Athenian siege of Paros in 489 BC after Marathon.
The Parian Chronicle, a marble stele of 264/263 BC, records events from legendary times in a year-by-year list.
The sculptor Scopas was born on Paros.

milestones.text: The Parian Chronicle is bought in Asia Minor for the Earl of Arundel's collection.

summary: A Cycladic island famous for its pure white marble, the birthplace of the poet Archilochus and the sculptor Scopas.
significance: The source of the finest sculptural marble of the ancient world.
body:
Paros, in the central Cyclades, was among the wealthiest islands of the archaic Aegean. Its marble, quarried from underground galleries and prized for its translucency, was used by sculptors across Greece, and the Nike of Samothrace is carved from it.

The poet Archilochus, who wrote of soldiering, love and satire, was born there about 680 BC and took part in the colonisation of Thasos. After Marathon, the Athenian general Miltiades laid siege to Paros for twenty-six days, because the island had sided with the Persians, and withdrew wounded and unsuccessful.

The Parian Chronicle, carved about 264/263 BC, gives a chronological list of events from the age of Cecrops to its own day. Part of it was acquired in 1627 for the Earl of Arundel, and fragments are now in Oxford and Paros.

name: Melos

claims.text: Melos was the main source of obsidian in the Aegean from the Neolithic onward.
The Bronze Age town of Phylakopi on the north coast was a major Cycladic centre influenced by Minoan and Mycenaean culture.
In 416 BC Athens captured Melos, killed the men and enslaved the women and children, after the debate that Thucydides records as the Melian dialogue.
The Venus de Milo was found on the island in 1820.

milestones.text: A farmer finds the statue of Aphrodite later known as the Venus de Milo.

summary: A volcanic Cycladic island, rich in obsidian, whose conquest by Athens in 416 BC is the subject of the Melian dialogue.
significance: The source of the Aegean's obsidian, the findspot of the Venus de Milo, and the scene of one of the most notorious atrocities of the Peloponnesian War.
body:
Melos is a volcanic island at the south-western end of the Cyclades. Its obsidian, a glassy rock which can be chipped to a razor edge, was traded across the Aegean from the Neolithic period, and the island has been settled since the seventh millennium BC. The Bronze Age town of Phylakopi, on the north coast, shows successive Cycladic, Minoan and Mycenaean phases.

In the Peloponnesian War, Melos stayed neutral, though it was a Spartan colony. In 416 BC Athens sent a force and demanded its submission. Thucydides stages the negotiation as a debate in which the Melians appeal to justice and the Athenians answer that the strong do what they can and the weak accept what they must. The Melians refused, the city fell after a siege, and the Athenians killed the men of military age and enslaved the rest.

In 1820 a farmer unearthed the statue now known as the Venus de Milo near the ancient theatre. The island is also known for its catacombs, which are early Christian burial chambers.

name: Thasos

claims.text: Parian colonists, among them the poet Archilochus, settled Thasos around 680–650 BC.
The island and its mainland possessions had gold and silver mines that made it rich.
Thasos revolted from the Delian League in 465 BC and was reduced by Athens after a siege of about two years.
The painter Polygnotus came from Thasos.

summary: A northern Aegean island colonised from Paros in the seventh century BC, rich in gold, wine and marble, whose revolt from Athens in 465 BC lasted two years.
significance: A wealthy colony whose resources and defiance of Athens made it a test case for the Delian League.
body:
Thasos lies off the Thracian coast, near the mouth of the Nestos. Settlers from Paros, including the poet Archilochus, colonised it in the 680s–650s BC to exploit the gold of the island and of the mainland opposite, where the Thasians also founded towns. The island was also known for its wine and marble.

When Thasos joined the Delian League, a quarrel with Athens over the Thracian mines led it to leave in 465 BC. Athens sent Cimon with a fleet and besieged the city for about two years. Thasos had to demolish its walls, surrender its fleet and mainland holdings, and pay tribute. Sparta had promised to invade Attica to aid it, but an earthquake and helot revolt prevented this.

The island's markets, harbour and walls survive, and its gates carry reliefs of divine figures. The painter Polygnotus came from Thasos. The French School at Athens has dug there since 1911.

name: Euboea

claims.text: Euboea is the second-largest Greek island, a long strip lying along the east coast of central Greece, separated from the mainland by the narrow Euripus channel.
Euboean traders, among them settlers from Chalcis and Eretria, were the first to reach the Levant and the west in the early Iron Age.
The Euboeans founded Pithekoussai and Cumae in Italy, and many colonies in Chalcidice.
Naval actions at Artemisium on the north coast of Euboea accompanied Thermopylae in 480 BC.
Euboea revolted from Athens in 446 BC and was reconquered by Pericles.

summary: The long island off the east coast of central Greece, home of the trading cities Chalcis and Eretria and of the earliest Greek contacts with the Levant and Italy.
significance: The island that led the Greek recovery after the Dark Age and opened the sea routes west.
body:
Euboea is a long, mountainous island lying along the east coast of Attica and Boeotia. At the narrowest point of the Euripus channel, ships could pass only with the tide, and a bridge connects the island to the mainland near Chalcis.

In the tenth and ninth centuries BC, Euboeans, notably the people of Lefkandi, traded with Cyprus and the Levant, and Euboean pottery has been found at Al Mina in Syria and in Italy. The cities of Chalcis and Eretria founded colonies in Chalcidice, on Sicily and in southern Italy, where Pithekoussai and Cumae transmitted their alphabet to Italy. The Lelantine War between the two main cities is the first conflict in Greek tradition to involve other states.

In the Persian Wars, Eretria was destroyed in 490 BC and a naval battle was fought at Artemisium in 480. After the island joined the Athenian Empire, it rose against Athens in 446 BC, but Pericles crossed with an army and reconquered it. The island fell to Philip II in the fourth century.

name: Ithaca

claims.text: The modern island of Ithaca (Ithaki) in the Ionian Sea is the traditional home of Odysseus.
Some scholars have argued that Homer's Ithaca was actually Leucas or the Paliki peninsula of Kefalonia.
Bronze Age and later remains have been found at several sites on the island, among them a cave at Polis with offerings to Odysseus.
Ithaca was a small, poor island in the historical period, within the sphere of Corinth and Corcyra.

milestones.text: Heinrich Schliemann digs on Ithaca in search of the palace of Odysseus.

summary: The small Ionian island that Greek tradition identifies as the home of Odysseus, though the match with Homer's description is debated.
significance: The island whose name became a symbol of home and the journey back to it.
body:
Ithaca is a narrow, rocky island in the Ionian Sea, off the west coast of Greece, near Kefalonia. It is the traditional homeland of Odysseus, and the *Odyssey* is built around his twenty years' absence from it. By the classical period the island was identified as Homer's Ithaca, and the Polis cave, where offerings to Odysseus were left, supports a local hero-cult from at least Hellenistic times.

Homer's description does not fit the modern island in all details. He says Ithaca lies furthest to the west and describes its position relative to nearby islands in obscure terms. For this reason some scholars, from Wilhelm Dörpfeld in the early twentieth century, have placed Odysseus' home on Leucas, and others on the Paliki peninsula of Kefalonia. Ancient writers did not question Ithaca's identity, and Schliemann dug there in 1868.

In historical times Ithaca was a small and modest community. Its modern fame comes from the epic, and from Cavafy's poem which makes it a symbol of the purpose of travel.

name: Corcyra

claims.text: Corinthian colonists founded Corcyra around 734 BC, according to tradition under Chersicrates.
It became a naval power that quarrelled with its mother city, and fought one of the earliest recorded Greek sea battles with Corinth.
Athens' alliance with Corcyra in 433 BC and the battle of Sybota between Corcyra and Corinth were among the causes of the Peloponnesian War.
A savage civil war divided the city in 427 BC, which Thucydides describes as an example of how war corrupts a society.
A pediment of about 580 BC from the temple of Artemis shows a large Gorgon flanked by beasts.

milestones.text: Wilhelm Dörpfeld's excavation uncovers the Gorgon pediment of the temple of Artemis.

summary: A Corinthian colony on the island of Corfu that became a naval power, quarrelled with Corinth and pulled Athens into the events leading to the Peloponnesian War.
significance: The quarrel between Corcyra and Corinth was a direct cause of the Peloponnesian War, and its civil war of 427 BC became Thucydides' picture of political breakdown.
body:
Corcyra, modern Corfu, was founded by Corinth around 734 BC, and was positioned on the route to Italy and Sicily. The colony grew powerful, kept a large fleet, and was at odds with its mother city from early on.

In 435–433 BC a dispute over the colony of Epidamnus led to war between Corcyra and Corinth. Corcyra appealed to Athens, which made a defensive alliance with it and sent ships to the battle of Sybota in 433 BC. Corinth, angered, pressed Sparta to declare war on Athens. In 427 BC, democrats and oligarchs fought in Corcyra with great cruelty, and Thucydides saw in it the pattern for civil strife everywhere.

The city's most famous monument is the Gorgon pediment of its temple of Artemis, about 580 BC, found at Garitsa in 1911 and now in the Corfu museum. In antiquity some identified the island with Homer's Scheria, home of the Phaeacians.
